Columbiana County by the numbers

Columbiana County ranks 27 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 101,203 people in 46,133 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $139,100, the median home value sits 24% below the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Columbiana County reports $58,474. Owner-occupancy is 73%, so renters hold about 27% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1964, about 59 years ago.

Who files a deed for a Columbiana County house?

The Columbiana County Recorder files them, at the courthouse in Lisbon. The recorder's website gives 330-424-9517 as the office number. Ohio's section 5301.25 sends every deed to the recorder of the county that holds the land, and it adds a warning: a deed left off the record is treated as fraudulent toward a later purchaser who never heard of it. For a seller, that makes the filing the last step of the sale.

What the office keeps is wider than deeds. Its home page lists mortgages, easements and military discharge papers, and it says new filings are recorded and searchable immediately. Originals come back to whoever submitted them after the staff finish quality control. The same page offers copies of plats and old maps in sizes from 8 by 11 up to 36 by 80, priced from $2 to $5 depending on the paper.

What fees apply when a Columbiana County deed is filed?

The recorder, the auditor and, where it is levied, the county each charge their own rate. The recorder's Documents and Fees page says the state schedule has two equal parts, one for the recorder and one for the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, and that a county may tack on a preservation surcharge of up to $5 whose amount differs from county to county. Phone the office for the Columbiana figure before the closing.

ItemRate stated in the Ohio Revised Code
Deed filing, pages one and two (section 317.32)$17 recorder fee and $17 housing trust fund fee
Every further page (section 317.32)$4 recorder fee and $4 housing trust fund fee
Preservation surcharge (section 317.32)Up to $5, county decides
Auditor's conveyance fee (section 319.54)The greater of $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value
Auditor's entry fee (section 319.54)50 cents per transfer
County transfer tax, if levied (section 322.02)No more than 30 cents per $100 of value

Whether the commissioners levy the county transfer tax is a question for the Columbiana County Auditor. The figure above is a ceiling written into the statute, not a promise that it applies here.

Why does the auditor see a Columbiana County deed first?

Because the auditor moves the parcel into the buyer's name on the tax list and endorses the deed before it goes to the recorder. Section 319.202 has the buyer file a value statement, and it makes the seller pay the conveyance fee. Value here includes any mortgage balance that stays on the property.

The form asks two things that suit this county's mix of town lots and farms. One is whether the property carried an owner-occupancy or homestead tax reduction. The other is whether the land was enrolled in the agricultural use valuation program, and what happens to the recoupment charge if it leaves. Sellers of acreage in the northern townships should expect that second question.

The statute also lists transfers that owe no conveyance fee. Examples include:

  • Gifts within a marriage or from parent to child
  • Splits between heirs when nobody pays money
  • Corrective deeds that fix an earlier one
  • Moves into or out of a revocable trust by its maker

The reason for any exemption goes on the value statement, so write it down before you visit the auditor in Lisbon.

What must a deed show before the auditor accepts it?

Section 5301.01 requires the seller's signature, acknowledged before a judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer, notary or mayor. A notary at your bank or title company covers that. Under section 319.20 the auditor also wants these in hand:

  • A mailing address for at least one buyer
  • The volume and page, or other marker, of the seller's own deed
  • A legal description that lines up with the tax list

When only part of a parcel changes hands, the auditor divides the tax value between the piece sold and the piece kept. Any back taxes on the original parcel are then shared out by value if the buyer or the remaining owner asks.

Where is Columbiana County and what shaped its housing?

The county lies on Ohio's eastern edge. Pennsylvania is on its east side, Mahoning County on the north, and about 20 miles of Ohio River frontage on the south. The county's own history page counts 534 square miles and 18 townships. The glacier's southern limit crosses the county near Lisbon, so the north is level, fertile farmland and the south is hilly, with limestone soils better for pasture, orchards and timber.

Settlement came early. Cabins went up in St. Clair Township around 1792 or 1793, and the legislature organized the county on March 25, 1803, the same year a Baptist minister platted Lisbon as New Lisbon. The word New was dropped in 1895. Towns followed the river, the Sandy and Beaver Canal and then the railroads: Wellsville in 1797, East Liverpool in 1798 and Salem in 1806. East Liverpool became a pottery center after 1839, and Salem later built pumps and auto bodies.

By the 2020 census Salem was the largest city at 11,915 people, then East Liverpool at 9,958 and Columbiana at 6,559. Lisbon counted 2,597 and East Palestine 4,761. East Palestine is also where a freight train derailed on February 3, 2023 and is part of the county's recent history.

What do the Census figures say about Columbiana County homes?

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for the county lists the following:

  • 99,377 residents at the July 1, 2025 estimate, 2.5% below the April 2020 estimate base
  • 46,220 housing units and 41,459 households
  • 72.7% of homes owner-occupied
  • Median home value of $151,600 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median rent of $756 a month
  • Median household income of $58,180
  • 58 building permits in 2025

Those are countywide medians. A house on a village street in Lisbon and a farmhouse in Madison Township will sit far apart, so use a written offer or local appraisal for the real number on your own property.

What can a seller line up before heading to Lisbon?

Most of this is a phone call each:

  • Ask the county treasurer what is owed on the parcel so the title company can clear it from the proceeds
  • Ask any lender to record a release of an old mortgage
  • If the owner has died, ask the probate court which papers allow a sale and who signs
  • Match the legal description on your deed to the tax record
  • Agree on who covers any farm-use recoupment or open assessment

The same route applies when a house is sold as-is for cash. The deed still passes through the auditor first and the recorder second, in the same order. Salem, East Liverpool, Columbiana and the villages all file in the same Lisbon office, so a seller in Wellsville or Leetonia does not need a separate local filing. Bring the signed deed, the completed value statement and a way to pay each office, and ask at the counter how the recorder and the auditor want the payments handed in.

More questions about Columbiana County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Can I reach the Columbiana County Recorder by phone?

Yes. The recorder's website gives 330-424-9517 for the office, which is based at the courthouse in Lisbon.

What is the preservation surcharge on a deed filed in Columbiana County?

State law lets a county charge up to $5 per document, and the recorder's site says the amount varies by county. Ask the office for the current Columbiana County charge.

Does the buyer or the seller pay the conveyance fee?

The seller pays it under section 319.202, while the buyer files the statement of value. If the county levies a transfer tax, the seller pays that as well.

Can relatives transfer a house without the conveyance fee?

Often, yes. Section 319.54 exempts gifts between spouses or between a parent and child, and splits among heirs when no money is paid. The reason must be stated on the value statement.

What if the deed is signed but never filed?

The deed is still a signed document, but section 5301.25 treats it as fraudulent against a later purchaser with no knowledge of it. Filing with the recorder closes that gap.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Statewide statutory base recording fee (ORC 317.32): $34 first two pages ($17 base + $17 housing trust fund) and $8 each additional page, plus document preservation surcharge up to $5 deposited to county general fund

Crawford County by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts 41,767 people and 19,844 housing units in Crawford County, which ranks 60 of 63 oh counties here. Median home value is $123,600, which is 33% below the middle county in this oh set. Households here earn a median $55,477; the middle oh county is at $69,699. 29% of occupied homes are rented, which leaves 71% owner-occupied. The median home was built in 1958, about 65 years ago.

Where does a Crawford County deed get recorded?

At the Crawford County Recorder's office in Bucyrus, the county seat. The recorder's website calls the office the official land records office for all real estate in Crawford County, and it lists 419-562-6961 as the number to call. The office follows sections 317.11 and 317.112 of the Ohio Revised Code, which set what a document must look like before staff accept it.

One local rule surprises people. According to the recorder's FAQ, a document that transfers real estate has to be approved first, and that process starts at the Crawford County Engineer's office, not at the recorder. The recorder also points out that its staff cannot give legal advice, so it suggests an attorney or title agency prepare the deed. Fill-in-the-blank forms exist, but the office stresses that the person submitting them is responsible for meeting every legal requirement.

What fees does the Bucyrus recorder print for a deed?

The recorder's fee page announces a $5 increase that took effect January 1, 2025 under Senate Bill 94, bringing the standard recording fee to $39 for the first two pages and $8 for each page after that. The office notes that each printed side counts as one page, and that $4 reference fees and the office's standardization guidelines still apply. The page-by-page figures it prints are:

Pages in the deedRecorder's fee
1 or 2$39.00
3$47.00
4$55.00
5$63.00
6$71.00
10$103.00

A few other items on the same schedule can come up in a sale. A release of a lien costs $4, a federal tax lien filing costs $5, and a document carrying a marginal notation adds $4 per notation to the regular fee. Plats and condominium drawings are priced by area, at $0.10 per square inch with a $40 minimum per page. The checklist asks filers to bring separate checks for the recorder, the auditor and the treasurer.

What does the Crawford County Recorder want to see on a deed?

The recorder publishes an eleven-point guide, and these are the points that trip up sellers most often:

  • The document must be an original, signed and notarized
  • A deed prepared in Ohio must carry a prepared-by statement
  • It must include the complete legal description, which the office uses for geographic indexing
  • Later documents should cite the book and page of earlier recordings
  • Exhibits and schedules must be clearly identified
  • The preparer's name and address, a return address and a phone number for minor fixes should appear
  • A self-addressed stamped envelope gets the original back without postage charges

The office adds that it is the filer's job to make sure pages are legible enough to scan. The checklist ends with a reminder to review the work, especially the fees, to avoid rejection.

When it indexes a deed, the office searches by legal description rather than street address. If you only have the house number, the recorder's FAQ says to find the owner name and transfer date through the Crawford County Auditor's search page first.

What does the Crawford County Auditor add to a sale?

The auditor sets the value that tax bills rest on and receives the conveyance paperwork. Its real estate page says property is revalued every three years under Ohio Department of Taxation rules, that taxes are figured on 35% of market value, and that Crawford County has 54 taxing districts, each with its own rate. No owner pays more than 10 mills of unvoted levies, and the voted portion depends on local elections.

Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement and the seller pays the conveyance fee, plus any county transfer tax that the commissioners have levied under section 322.02. The statutory conveyance fee is $1 or 10 cents per $100, whichever is greater, according to section 319.54. Ask the Crawford County Auditor which county rate applies, since the statute only caps it at 30 cents per $100.

The auditor's page also describes several items that matter to a seller:

  • Owners may contest a value from January 1 to March 31 before the Board of Revision
  • New construction or an improvement over $2,000 must be reported, and failure can bring a 50% penalty on the owner's taxes
  • Building permits are issued by the cities of Bucyrus and Galion, Jackson, Jefferson and Polk townships, and the villages of Crestline, New Washington, North Robinson and Chatfield
  • Farmland in the current agricultural use value program pays a one-time $25 enrollment fee
  • Manufactured home buyers have 30 days to register with the auditor, or face a $100 penalty

What is Crawford County like for a home seller?

Crawford County sits in north central Ohio. Wikipedia lists it as the fourth smallest county in the state by total area, at 403 square miles, with the Sandusky and Olentangy rivers draining it. Bucyrus is the county seat and largest city, and Galion is the other city. The county is named for Colonel William Crawford, and it makes up the Bucyrus micropolitan area. Neighbors are Seneca, Huron, Richland, Morrow, Marion and Wyandot counties.

The county's population peaked at 50,364 in 1970 and counted 42,025 in 2020, with the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate at 41,896. Public libraries in Bucyrus, Galion and Crestline serve the county. In the 2020 census, 65.9% of residents lived in urban areas and 34.1% in rural areas, a split that explains why a Bucyrus lot and a township farmhouse can be priced so differently.

How do Crawford County homes compare on the numbers?

QuickFacts, the Census Bureau's county profile, prints these figures for Crawford:

  • Typical owner-occupied home value: $136,700 in the 2020 to 2024 survey
  • Owner-occupied rate: 73.1%
  • Housing units: 19,813, with 18,059 households
  • Median gross rent: $794
  • Median household income: $58,044, with 11.2% of people in poverty
  • Building permits in 2025: 3
  • Median owner cost with a mortgage: $1,081 a month, and $487 without one

Only three building permits were counted for 2025, so housing here is mostly what already stands. A written cash offer or a local appraisal can price a particular house more reliably than a countywide median can. Sellers in Galion, Crestline, Bucyrus and the townships all record in the same Bucyrus office.

What should be settled before heading to Bucyrus?

The recorder's FAQ makes clear that it does not release liens. It records them, and the Treasurer or the Clerk of Courts handles the underlying tax and court filings. That means a seller should sort out the following with the right office before the deed is filed:

  • Ask the County Treasurer for the unpaid tax figure so the title company can pay it from the proceeds
  • Ask a lender to file a release of any old mortgage, since the recorder only records it
  • Check with the Clerk of Courts for judgments tied to the owner
  • Ask the County Engineer's office about the transfer approval step
  • Match the legal description to the one on your last deed

The same steps apply when the buyer is paying cash and the house is sold as-is.

More questions about Crawford County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the phone number for the Crawford County Recorder?

The office number printed on the recorder's website is 419-562-6961. The office is in Bucyrus.

How much does it cost to record a three-page deed in Crawford County?

The recorder's fee table prints $47.00 for three pages. That is $39 for the first two pages and $8 for the third, before any other charges the document triggers.

Does the recorder remove liens from my title?

No. The office only records certain liens and says it does not remove or release them. Property tax liens go through the County Treasurer, and court matters through the Clerk of Courts.

Where does the transfer process start in Crawford County?

At the County Engineer's office, according to the recorder's FAQ. A document that transfers real estate has to be approved there before it moves on.

Can I search records by street address at the recorder?

Not directly. The recorder indexes by legal description, so look up the owner name or transfer date on the County Auditor's search page if you only have an address.

What we could not confirm

    Darke County by the numbers

    Darke County has about 51,655 residents and 22,643 housing units in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, number 49 by population among the 63 oh counties we cover. The median owner-occupied home is worth $169,100, 8% below the median of the oh counties covered. Median household income is $64,654, against $69,699 for the middle oh county. Owners live in 72% of occupied homes and renters in 28%. The median home was built in 1963, about 60 years ago.

    Which office files a Darke County deed?

    The Darke County Recorder files it. The office sits in the Greenville courthouse at 504 S. Broadway, answers at 937-547-7390, and posts weekday hours from 8 to 4.

    ORC Chapter 317 governs the office, which the county describes as its official keeper of records. Besides deeds and mortgages, the recorder takes mechanic liens, powers of attorney, recognizance bonds, IRS liens, corporate franchise liens and partnership papers. The job is to record what you bring, so a deed written by you or your attorney needs to be finished before it arrives.

    What must be done to a deed before the recorder accepts it?

    A deed needs the grantor's signature, an acknowledgment, and the auditor's stamp before it goes to the recorder. Under ORC 5301.01, the grantor acknowledges the signing before a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, and that official certifies the acknowledgment.

    In Darke County the usual order runs like this:

    1. Draft the deed with a legal description that matches the parcel. The county engineer keeps the tax maps and reviews deeds, land transfers and lot splits for proper boundary descriptions.
    2. Sign and acknowledge the deed.
    3. Take the deed and a conveyance fee statement to the Darke County Auditor on the courthouse first floor. The auditor's forms page lists DTE 100 for a standard conveyance, DTE 100EX for an exempt one, DTE 101 for homestead property and DTE 102 for farmland valued at its agricultural use.
    4. Pay the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax to the auditor, get the stamp, and bring the deed to the recorder.

    Bring these to the auditor's counter:

    • The signed and acknowledged deed with its legal description.
    • A completed conveyance fee statement on the right DTE form.
    • Payment for the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax.

    Splitting a lot off a larger parcel adds a step. The county's own contact list sends split questions to the zoning inspector at 937-547-7381, and building permits for the unincorporated areas, the city of Greenville and a list of villages run through the county building regulation office at 937-547-7379.

    What are the Darke County recording charges?

    The schedule comes from ORC 317.32. A standard deed or mortgage pays $17 plus a matching $17 housing trust fund fee through page two, then $4 plus $4 for every further page. Counties may add a preservation surcharge of as much as $5 a document. Ask the recorder whether Darke County collects it, and how much.

    StepOfficeWhat you leave with
    Boundary checkCounty engineerSign-off on the legal description
    Value statement and feesCounty auditorStamped deed
    FilingCounty recorderRecorded instrument

    The same statute prices copies. A certified copy costs a $1 base fee and a $1 housing trust fund fee per page, a recorder's seal on the certification adds $0.50 and $0.50, and a marginal reference entered through a separate instrument costs $2 and $2. Charges fall due when the paper is presented, and each page, caption page included, counts at its 8.5 by 14 inch size or fraction of one (ORC 317.32).

    Which side of a Darke County sale pays the transfer costs?

    The seller. ORC 319.202(D) assigns the grantor the conveyance fee under section 319.54(G)(3), and also any transfer tax the commissioners adopted under Chapter 322. A county transfer tax may not exceed thirty cents per hundred dollars of value and is paid to the auditor before recording (ORC 322.02). Ask the Darke County auditor if one is in place.

    For a sale, value means the full price paid or to be paid, mortgage or vendor's lien included. For a gift it means the likely open-market price, and willful falsification is prohibited. The auditor's site offers a calculator that takes a parcel count and sale price and includes the parcel transfer fee, so test the figure before closing.

    What does the Darke County auditor check on a deed?

    The stamp is the auditor's way of telling the recorder that the paperwork is complete. ORC 319.202 has the buyer or the buyer's representative file the value statement. The auditor then marks the deed with the fee and compliance, keeps the original, and sends the tax commissioner a copy that notes the latest assessed value.

    Two sets of affirmations ride on that statement. The first covers a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the current or prior year's tax. The second covers agricultural valuation. If the answer to either is yes, both sides sign a sworn instrument that accounts for the reduction or for the recoupment charge. For residential rental property, the indorsement also reminds the buyer of landlord information due under ORC 5323.02.

    For a family transfer or other exempt deed, the statement only needs the reason for the exemption. Pick the exempt form (DTE 100EX) and state the reason plainly.

    How far back do online Darke County land records reach?

    The recorder's page offers an online search of land records beginning May 1996 and says the index was due to reach back to January 1980 by the end of 2023. Ask the office how far back it runs now, and how to view older books in person.

    A free Property Fraud Alert subscription is also on offer. It is a notification service that warns an owner when a document is recorded against the property, and it suits anyone holding a vacant house.

    • Parcel searches, the county map and the sales report live on the auditor's website, not at the recorder.
    • Questions about value or tax on a parcel go to the auditor, and questions about what is already of record go to the recorder.

    What history and roads frame Darke County land records?

    Settlement began at Fort Jefferson in 1791, and the Treaty of Greenville was signed at Fort Greenville in 1795, ceding southern Ohio to the United States. Darke County was created in 1809 and organized in 1817, the first railroad reached it in 1850, and by the late twentieth century the economy mixed farming with manufacturing while many residents commuted to Dayton.

    The 2020 census found 51,881 residents, a median age of 42.5, and 20.8 percent of people at least 65. It counted 20,925 households, 28.8 percent of them one-person households. Land that families have held for decades makes the legal description important, and the county engineer reviews deeds for proper boundary descriptions.

    The county's villages include Ansonia, Arcanum, Castine, Gettysburg, Ithaca, New Madison, New Weston, Pitsburg, Union City, Versailles, Wayne Lakes and Yorkshire, and cities, villages and townships hold the zoning authority for their own ground. Main roads include US 127, US 36 and State Routes 49, 47, 121 and 118. Public school districts reaching into the county include Greenville City, Versailles Exempted Village, Ansonia Local, Arcanum-Butler Local, Bradford Exempted Village, Mississinawa Valley Local, Tri-Village Local and National Trail Local, among others, and a deed's parcel record shows the district for tax purposes. A house in an unzoned township answers to the township trustees on zoning, so confirm that before you list.

    More questions about Darke County, OH Recorder of Deeds

    How do I reach the Darke County Recorder?

    Call 937-547-7390 or go to the courthouse at 504 S. Broadway in Greenville. The county lists the office as open on weekdays.

    Is the Darke County filing charge based on page count?

    Yes. Ohio sets one price for the first two pages and a lower price per added page, and a preservation surcharge of up to $5 may apply on top. ORC 317.32 has the list.

    Which comes first in Darke County, auditor or recorder?

    The auditor. The conveyance fee statement and fee earn the stamp, and the recorder then files the stamped deed.

    Is a homemade deed acceptable in Darke County?

    It can be brought in, but it needs a signature, an acknowledgment before an authorized official, a description the engineer's tax maps support and the auditor's stamp. A title company or attorney can prepare it.

    Can older Darke County deeds be found online?

    Online search starts with May 1996. The recorder planned to extend the index to January 1980, so ask what year it begins now.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Statewide statutory base recording fee (ORC 317.32): $34 first two pages ($17 base + $17 housing trust fund) and $8 each additional page, plus document preservation surcharge up to $5 deposited to county general fund
  • Effective January 1, 2025 additional $5 per-document preservation fee on top of $34 first 2 pages and $8 each additional; cash or check only; $4 marginal notation fee

Fees

Selling in Defiance County?
We buy Defiance County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What we could not confirm

    What is the Defiance County Recorder responsible for?

    Every paper that conveys or burdens land in Defiance County ends up in the recorder's permanent files. The office also takes military discharge papers (DD214s), secures them from public view, and issues free veteran ID cards to honorably discharged veterans without an appointment.

    Filing is the office's job. It does not run searches for the public, confirm on your behalf that a mortgage was cancelled, or prepare liens. Anyone may come in and search the public records themselves, and staff will help, and an online document index lets a seller look for a recorded mortgage release before listing.

    Landowners can also sign up for a free property fraud alert at propertyfraudalert.com, or by using the hotline number the recorder prints on its page.

    What are the Defiance County recording charges?

    The office lists $34 for the first two pages of a document and $8 for each page after those. A $5 document preservation fee joined the schedule on January 1, 2025, following Ohio Senate Bill 94, which took effect October 24, 2024 and let counties charge up to that amount per document.

    Papers with their own statutory fees skip the extra $5; the recorder names federal tax liens, state job and family services liens, plats, township zoning documents and UCCs. Recording is paid in cash or by check only.

    ItemDefiance County charge
    Pages one and two together$34
    Every page after page two$8
    Document preservation fee, from January 1, 2025$5 per document
    Marginal notation on a release or assignment$4
    Copies made by the public$0.25 per copy
    Auditor's conveyance fee$4.00 per thousand
    Auditor's transfer fee$0.50 per parcel

    Sources: the recorder's page and the auditor's deed transfer page. A page counts for the fee if it has writing on it.

    Which approvals does a Defiance County deed need first?

    Sellers start at the auditor, because no deed reaches the recorder without the auditor's stamp. The auditor's deed transfer page lays out the sequence.

    1. The county engineer's office checks the legal description, locates the parcel on the tax maps and stamps its approval with a date and signature. The recorder's page gives the engineer's number as 419-782-4751.
    2. For certain splits or subdivisions of less than 20 acres, or with a leftover parcel under 20 acres, the Defiance County Planning Commission must also approve.
    3. A conveyance form travels with the deed. A sale for money pays $4.00 per $1000 at transfer unless an exemption applies, and any deed moving an interest, exempt or not, adds $0.50 for each parcel number.
    4. The auditor confirms that the grantor matches the tax duplicate and that the descriptions agree, then stamps the deed with the fee collected and the parcel count.
    5. The stamped deed goes to the recorder.

    A land split adds a tax step. After the engineer approves it, the real estate assessors in the auditor's office work out the tax effect of the split, looking at items such as buildings being transferred and any current agricultural use recoupment charge that may apply to the land. Where a split would leave a parcel under 20 acres, expect the planning commission to be involved too.

    Bring these on the day you record:

    • The stamped deed with its fee paid at the auditor.
    • Cash or a check for the recording charge.
    • A self-addressed stamped envelope if you want the original mailed back.

    Call the auditor at 419-782-1926 about conveyance requirements before recording, and 419-784-3111 for property value, sales history and tax questions.

    What page and margin rules apply to a Defiance County deed?

    Check the paper against the recorder's list before you carry it in. A printed or typed name must sit beside each signature, and a "prepared by" line must appear (ORC 317.11). Notary seals must be present, the whole document must be in English or come with a certified translation, and pages must reproduce legibly.

    • Ink is black or blue, type is at least 10 point, and nothing is highlighted.
    • The first page keeps a three-inch blank band at the top; later pages keep one and a half inches.
    • All pages keep one inch clear at the bottom and both sides.
    • Sheets run from 8.5 by 11 up to 8.5 by 14 inches.
    • A self-addressed stamped envelope goes in for the return.

    The county engineer must approve some legal descriptions before recording, and releases and assignments need a legal description. Reference earlier recorded documents when a marginal notation is needed. The office lists a turnaround of three days.

    How do the Defiance County fees relate to the Ohio statute?

    The county's $34 and $8 figures are the sum of two statutory pieces. ORC 317.32 sets a base fee of $17 for the first two pages plus a $17 housing trust fund fee, and $4 plus $4 for each page after that. The recorder's page says the office forwards the housing trust fund share on a quarterly basis and divides the rest between the general fund and the technology fund.

    The statute also names smaller items that a seller may meet during a sale. A certified copy costs a base fee of $1 plus a $1 housing trust fund fee per page, a recorder's seal on a certification adds $0.50 plus $0.50, and a marginal reference entered by a separate instrument costs $2 plus $2. Defiance County lists a flat $4 for marginal notations on a release or assignment, so ask the office which figure applies to a mortgage release you plan to record.

    Because recording is by mail often, the practical points are short. Send cash or a check, add a self-addressed stamped envelope, and allow the three days the office lists for turnaround. The fee schedule is posted on the recorder's page, and a call to the office confirms the total before you mail anything.

    What is Defiance County like for a seller?

    Defiance County sits in northwest Ohio along the Indiana line. It covers 414 square miles, of which about 411 are land, and it borders Williams, Henry, Putnam and Paulding counties in Ohio and Allen and DeKalb counties in Indiana. The city of Defiance is the county seat and largest city, named for the old fort that gave the county its name.

    The 2020 census counted 38,286 people and 16,539 housing units, with 6.4 percent of units vacant. Of occupied homes, 76.1 percent were owner-occupied and 23.9 percent rented. About 46.4 percent of residents lived in urban areas and 53.6 percent in rural ones, so a seller may hold a town lot or a house on acreage.

    Defiance has long been a manufacturing community, anchored for decades by a General Motors foundry that employed more than 5,000 people at its peak.

    The median age was 41.4 and 20.0 percent of residents were 65 or older. The count showed 15,482 households, of which 27.8 percent were one-person households. The county takes its name from Fort Defiance, an early army post named by Anthony Wayne, and the Defiance micropolitan area covers the whole county. Sellers who hold long-owned parcels should confirm legal descriptions with the engineer before a deed goes to the auditor, since that office will not transfer a deed without its approval stamp.

    More questions about Defiance County, OH Recorder of Deeds

    What will a Defiance County deed cost to file?

    Expect $34 for the first pair of pages, $8 for each page beyond those, and the $5 preservation fee in force since January 1, 2025. Pay with cash or a check.

    Does the auditor see a Defiance County deed first?

    Yes. The engineer approves the legal description, then the auditor collects its fees and stamps the deed, and only then does the recorder file it.

    What rate does the Defiance County auditor charge on a sale?

    The recorder's page prints $4.00 per thousand as the conveyance fee and $0.50 per parcel as the transfer fee. An exempt deed skips the first but still carries the second.

    Will the recorder's staff correct a flawed deed?

    No. The office may not engage in the unauthorized practice of law, which rules out drafting papers or giving legal advice. An attorney or title company should prepare the deed.

    Can I look up Defiance County records from home?

    Yes, through the online document index in AVA Land Records. A seller can use it to see if a mortgage release was recorded, then visit the office for anything the index lacks.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

The Delaware County recorder of deeds records Ohio deeds and mortgages.

Who records deeds in Delaware County

  • Delaware County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Statewide statutory base recording fee (ORC 317.32): $34 first two pages ($17 base + $17 housing trust fund) and $8 each additional page, plus document preservation surcharge up to $5 deposited to county general fund

Fees

Selling in Delaware County?
We buy Delaware County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • treasurer site, due dates, fees, millage
  • Delaware recorder homepage opened: no fee/e-recording text found

Delaware County by the numbers

Delaware County ranks 13 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 221,160 people in 84,215 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $419,500, the median home value sits 129% above the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Delaware County reports $130,088. Owner-occupancy is 78%, so renters hold about 22% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1999, about 24 years ago.

What does the Delaware County recorder do for a home seller?

The recorder's office, according to its own home page, indexes all real estate and personal property records for Delaware County, collects the filing fees, and keeps Military Service Discharge records. When a house sells, two papers land on its desk: the deed that gives the buyer title, and the satisfaction that shows the seller's lender has been paid.

Visit 145 N. Union St., Delaware, OH 43015, or call (740) 833-2460. Recordings are accepted on weekdays from 8:30 to 4:30 with holidays excluded, the cutoff for submitting documents is 4:00 p.m., and an exam room is open for the public during the same hours. The site also offers a recorded document search, a veterans graves search and a property fraud page.

What is the charge for filing a two-page deed in Delaware County?

Delaware County's fee page lists $39.00 for the first two pages of a deed, mortgage, lease, power of attorney, release or assignment on paper 8.5 by 14 inches or smaller, and $8.00 for every page after that. A footnote says the $39.00 already contains the $5.00 preservation surcharge permitted by ORC 317.32.

Recording and copy charges at the Delaware County Recorder (source: the recorder's Fees and Charges page)
Document or serviceCharge listed
Basic instrument, first 2 pages$39.00, then $8.00 per added page
Marginal reference on a release, amendment or assignment$4.00 each
Map, plat or print, recorded or certified$40.00 per page
Federal tax lien: original or release$5.00 or $3.00
Living will or health care power of attorney$40.00 flat per document
Photocopy, and certified copy$2.00 per page, and $2.00 per page plus $2.00 to certify
Veteran's dischargeNo fee

The statute behind these numbers, ORC 317.32, splits the first-two-pages price into a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee. Each added page carries $4 plus $4, and a county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. The recorder asks mailers to send a postage-paid return envelope or enough cash to cover the postage.

Which Delaware County office sees the deed before the recorder?

The auditor does. ORC 322.02 says that when a county levies a real property transfer tax, the grantor named in the deed pays it to the county auditor at delivery of the deed, ahead of presenting the deed to the recorder. The buyer also files a statement of value with the auditor under ORC 319.202 before the deed is endorsed.

The same statute caps a county's transfer tax at thirty cents per hundred dollars of value. The rate in force for Delaware County is a number to get from the auditor at (740) 833-2900 close to the closing date, since a county sets it by commissioners' resolution.

  • Auditor first: value statement, any transfer tax, and the endorsement on the deed.
  • Recorder second: the endorsed deed, the page-count fee, and a return envelope if the package is mailed.
  • Same building: both offices share 145 N. Union St., so a hand delivery needs only one trip.
  • Last stop: the online document search, to see that the deed shows against the right parcel.

What other papers does the recorder file besides deeds?

The fee schedule reads like a map of what can cloud or clear a title. Federal tax liens cost $5.00 to record in original, corrected, refiled, partial release or subordination form, and a release costs $3.00. Uniform Commercial Code filings such as fixture filings and continuation statements cost $12.00 plus $4.00 for each name indexed, and a UCC search costs $20.00.

Other entries a homeowner may meet include zoning resolutions at a $50.00 flat fee, zoning amendments at $20.00, attested accounts that place liens on public funds, a motor vehicle bond lien at $10.00, and Bureau of Workers' Compensation releases, which are free. A bill of sale in a bulk sale carries no fee either.

Ask the title company which of these appear against your name before you list. A federal tax lien or a stale mortgage that was never released can slow down a buyer's lender, and the recorder's online search will show what is on file.

How does the recorder describe a warranty deed and a quitclaim deed?

The recorder's Real Estate Recording page borrows definitions from a real estate dictionary. A general warranty deed is one where the grantor agrees to protect the grantee against any other claim to title and adds further promises. A special warranty deed narrows that promise to anyone claiming by, from, through or under the grantor, with no warranty against title defects from before the grantor owned the land.

A quitclaim deed passes along only what rights the grantor has, without naming those rights and without warranties of ownership. The page also defines recording as entering an instrument in the public books, which gives notice to the world. Which deed form a sale uses is up to the contract and the title agent, and the recorder's office does not pick it.

Which towns send deeds to the Delaware County recorder?

Every parcel in the county records here, whichever town it sits in. Wikipedia's county article lists the city of Delaware as the seat, along with Powell, Sunbury and the Delaware County portions of Dublin and Westerville. Villages include Ashley, Galena, Ostrander and Shawnee Hills, and Kilbourne and Radnor are census-designated places.

The county was formed from Franklin County in 1808, covers 443 square miles of land, and holds two reservoirs, Alum Creek Lake and Delaware Lake, on Alum Creek and the Olentangy River. The Columbus Zoo and Aquarium sits inside its borders, and Rutherford B. Hayes was born and raised in the county. Interstate 71 and US 23 are among the highways it lists, and the Delaware Municipal Airport serves the southern part of the county.

  • A deed for a Powell, Sunbury or Delaware house goes to the same recorder as one for a township farm.
  • Dublin and Westerville lie partly in other counties, so a mailing address in either one does not say which recorder applies; check the parcel record first.
  • The auditor's GIS property search shows which parcel number to cite on the paperwork.

What do the numbers say about Delaware County owners?

Headcount went from 174,214 in 2010 to 214,124 in 2020, and the bureau's 2025 estimate stands at 242,032. QuickFacts tallies 82,287 households over 2020 to 2024, and nine in ten residents (89.4%) were in the same home one year before being surveyed.

Ownership costs run high. Selected monthly owner costs have a median of $2,493 with a mortgage and $986 without; renters pay a median gross rent of $1,492. Workers travel an average of 25.4 minutes to their jobs. Ohio Wesleyan University, founded by Methodists in 1842, is in the city of Delaware, and Columbus State Community College opened a county campus in 2010.

More questions about Delaware County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the Delaware County recording fee for a three-page deed?

The schedule posts $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after that, so the third page is billed at the $8.00 rate. Marginal references on releases and assignments cost $4.00 each and are billed separately.

When must a document reach the Delaware County recorder?

The submission cutoff is 4:00 p.m., while the office itself works from 8:30 to 4:30 on weekdays. Holidays are excluded.

Does the Delaware County recorder charge for a veteran's discharge?

No. The fee schedule marks a veteran's discharge, and an expunged discharge, as no fee.

Who pays Delaware County's transfer tax at closing?

State law puts it on the grantor, meaning the seller named in the deed, and it goes to the auditor before recording. Ask the auditor's office at (740) 833-2900 what rate applies.

Can I look up Delaware County deeds from home?

Yes. The recorder's home page links a recorded document search, and a separate page searches veterans graves. Use it to check that your deed or a mortgage release was recorded.

Who records deeds in Erie County

  • Erie County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Statewide statutory base recording fee (ORC 317.32): $34 first two pages ($17 base + $17 housing trust fund) and $8 each additional page, plus document preservation surcharge up to $5 deposited to county general fund
  • Starting December 21, 2026 $5 Ohio preservation fee added: first 2 pages $39, $8 each additional page; e-recording vendors page and recording costs page linked

What we could not confirm

    Erie County by the numbers

    Erie County ranks 33 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 74,938 people in 38,400 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $183,900, the median home value sits 0% above the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Erie County reports $68,431. Owner-occupancy is 71%, so renters hold about 29% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1966, about 57 years ago.

    Where is the Erie County recorder, and what does it handle?

    The Erie County Recorder's Office is in the Erie County Office Building at 247 Columbus Avenue, Suite 225, Sandusky, OH 44870, phone (419) 627-7686. The counter is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. and closes for the usual holidays, including Juneteenth, Columbus Day and the day after Thanksgiving. When a holiday lands on a Saturday the office closes the Friday before, and a Sunday holiday means closing the Monday after.

    The office records deeds, mortgages, releases and similar papers, and it also takes military discharges. It is not a place to get paperwork drafted. Its FAQ says staff are not attorneys, keep no forms, run no lien or title searches, and cannot advise on how to prepare a legal document.

    What does recording a deed cost in Erie County?

    The recorder's pricing page says recording costs the same in every Ohio county and is charged by page: $34 total for the first two printed pages, then $8 for each page after that. A sheet printed on both sides counts as two pages. The page's own examples put a two-page document at $34 and a three-page one at $42.

    Erie County Recorder charges (source: recorder's Recording Costs page and Recorder FAQs)
    ItemWhat the page says
    First two printed pages$34 total
    Each page after the first two$8
    Marginal reference, such as an assignment or release$4 per document reference
    Affidavit for transfer (successor trustee)No $4 marginal fee
    Document that fails Ohio Revised Code standards$20 nonconformance fee
    Copies not available free online$2 per page

    Copy requests paid by card over the phone carry a processor charge, listed as a $2 minimum and up to 2 or 3 percent of the total, and American Express is not taken. The FAQ points out that every charge in the office is fixed by the Ohio Revised Code.

    What must an Erie County deed contain to be accepted?

    The Basic Recording Requirements page spells out what gets a document turned away. It asks for legible originals with original signatures, and it does not accept photocopies. The office checks a long list before it stamps anything.

    • A full legal description beginning "Situated in" the city or township, county and state, not the short description from the auditor's site or a tax bill.
    • A printed or typed name under every signature, and a full notary clause with the notary's stamp or printed name and the commission expiration date.
    • Both a first and last name for every party, with marital status; the page recommends the spouse of a married grantor sign and be notarized, even only to release dower.
    • A "Prepared By" line naming whoever drafted the document, and every attached exhibit that the document mentions.
    • No Social Security numbers or tax ID numbers; the office redacts the number on an original death certificate itself, and the certificate must stay unmarked.
    • For a signer acting under a power of attorney, the Erie County recording number of the power, or the power recorded just ahead of the deed in the same package.

    No white-out is allowed. The $20 nonconformance fee applies when a document misses these standards, which is why the office suggests stopping in first so staff can look it over.

    Can I mail a deed to the Erie County recorder or record it electronically?

    Deeds that transfer property cannot be mailed. The recorder's page says any document that transfers property, or a transfer on death designation or confirmation, must be stamped by the Transfer office, and it must be carried in or recorded electronically, not sent by mail, UPS or FedEx. The office says it can e-record almost every document type, transfer deeds included, for filers with an account at one of its listed vendors: ePN-eRecording Partners Network, Simplifile or CSC.

    Papers that do not need the Transfer stamp can come by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope large enough for everything. Each document goes through recording, indexing and verification before it is mailed back, and the office describes the usual turnaround as one to two business days before it goes out in the mail.

    What conveyance and transfer fees apply to an Erie County sale?

    The county auditor's Property Transfers page sets the conveyance fee at $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price, charged on real estate and on manufactured homes. A separate transfer fee is $0.50 per line. The auditor's rate history shows $1 per $1,000 from May 1969 to March 1990, rising in steps to $4 per $1,000 since February 1994.

    Exemptions need to meet a qualification on the state's DTE 100EX form, and the auditor's site has a Conveyance Fee Calculator that asks for the number of properties and the sale amount. The auditor's office is at 247 Columbus Avenue, Room 210, phone (419) 627-7746. Ask the recorder's staff where to get the Transfer stamp before you walk a deed to Suite 225.

    How do I find a recorded deed or a mortgage release in Erie County?

    Start with the free online search at the county's self-service site. The recorder's FAQ says indexing and images go back to 1990, with older documents being added, and a viewer can download or print images for free. Enter the last name first, then the first name, such as Smith Jane, in the Both Names box.

    Two points in the FAQ help sellers. The recorder does not hold your deed: you receive the original recorded deed at purchase, and the office keeps copies only. A paid-off mortgage produces a separate release or satisfaction, so a seller who cannot find proof of a payoff should look for that recorded document.

    What is Erie County like for a seller?

    Erie County sits on the Lake Erie shore, and 374 of its 626 square miles are water, which leaves 252 square miles of land. According to Wikipedia that makes it the second-smallest Ohio county by land area, behind Lake County. Sandusky is the seat and largest city, Huron and Vermilion are cities, and Bellevue and Vermilion lie partly within the county. The Huron and Vermilion rivers drain it, and Sandusky is known for limestone quarries. The 1872 courthouse at 323 Columbus Avenue was refaced in Art Deco style in the 1930s.

    The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 73,296 people, down 3.1% from 2020, and 26.8% are 65 or older. QuickFacts lists a typical owner-occupied home value of $199,700, household income at the midpoint of $71,993, and median gross rent of $933. Owners occupy 71.9% of homes and the average commute is 21.5 minutes. Sandusky City, Huron City, Vermilion, Perkins, Edison, Margaretta and Kelleys Island are among the school districts serving the county.

    How does Erie County property tax connect to the deed?

    The treasurer's FAQ says the county bills a year behind and that taxes follow the property, not the owner, so the balance on a parcel matters at closing. The auditor's site lists 2027 due dates of February 19 and July 16 for real estate bills, and the 2026 dates of February 18 and July 29 have passed. The treasurer's office is at 247 Columbus Avenue, Suite 115, phone (419) 627-7701.

    The treasurer's page on House Bill 186 sorts the county's school districts by whether parcels may get the Inflation Cap Credit.

    • May receive it: Bellevue, Edison, Firelands, Huron, Monroeville, Vermilion and Western Reserve.
    • Will not receive it: Kelleys Island, Margaretta, Perkins and Sandusky.
    • Homestead: the auditor lists a $40,000 household income threshold for applicants who are 65 or older or disabled.
    • Overdue parcels: sold only at sheriff's sale, according to the treasurer.

    More questions about Erie County, OH Recorder of Deeds

    How much does the Erie County recorder charge for a two-page deed?

    The charge is $34 for the first two printed pages. Each further page costs $8, and a document printed on both sides of one sheet counts as two pages.

    Can I mail an Erie County deed to the recorder?

    No, not if it transfers property. Those documents must be stamped by the Transfer office and delivered in person or recorded electronically through a listed vendor.

    What is the Erie County conveyance fee?

    The auditor's page lists $4.00 per thousand dollars of the sale price, plus a $0.50 per line transfer fee. Call the auditor at (419) 627-7746 to confirm figures for your closing.

    Does the Erie County recorder keep my original deed?

    No. The recorder's FAQ says it keeps copies only and that you receive the original recorded deed when you buy. A mortgage payoff produces its own release document.

    What time does the Erie County recorder open and close?

    The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Closed days include Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, the day after Thanksgiving and Christmas Day.

Fairfield County by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts 161,289 people and 63,397 housing units in Fairfield County, which ranks 20 of 63 oh counties here. Median home value is $272,200, which is 49% above the middle county in this oh set. Households here earn a median $87,069; the middle oh county is at $69,699. 26% of occupied homes are rented, which leaves 74% owner-occupied.

Where is the Fairfield County Recorder, and what does the office keep?

The Fairfield County Recorder works from the Administrative Courthouse at 210 East Main Street, Suite 205, in Lancaster, and keeps weekday hours of 8:00 am to 4:00 pm. The phone number is 740-652-7100. The office keeps the permanent public record of deeds, mortgages, leases, liens, plats, powers of attorney and military discharges for the county.

Indexes reach back to 1800, and scanned documents are searchable online from January 1980 forward. Staff will help you find the right desk, but they do not run searches for you, help draft a document, or hand out recording forms. A deed has to be written by someone else, such as a closing agent or an attorney.

  • Search deeds and mortgages through the Recorder's online land records link on the Recorder page.
  • Sign up for the free Property Fraud Alert and Notary Fraud Alert from the same page.
  • Call before a trip, because the page posts short closures such as a one-hour midday closing on a single day.

What must happen before a Fairfield County deed reaches the Recorder?

The deed goes to the County Auditor first, and only after the Auditor completes the transfer does it go to the Recorder. A Fairfield County sale usually needs two papers at the Auditor: the deed itself and a conveyance fee statement, which is Ohio form DTE 100 (or DTE 100EX when an exemption applies).

The Auditor's Map Room checks the legal description against the county conveyance standards before it accepts the deed. A prepared deed can be emailed to the Map Room for that approval, and the approval is a pre-requisite for the transfer. After approval, the deed and statement can be dropped at the transfer desk at 108 N. High Street in Lancaster, or mailed to the Auditor marked Attn: Conveyance.

Under Ohio law the buyer or the buyer's representative files the statement of value, and the seller pays the conveyance fee. The statement defines value as the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage included. For a gift, value is the estimated open market price. Writing a false value on purpose is prohibited by the statute (R.C. 319.202).

What will a Fairfield County deed transfer and recording run?

Two separate bills apply: the Auditor's transfer and conveyance charges, and the Recorder's page-based recording fee. The table lists the rates exactly as the official pages print them.

ChargeRate as publishedPaid to
Transfer fee$.50 per parcel, exempt and non-exempt transfers alikeCounty Auditor
Conveyance fee$4.00 per thousand of consideration when money changes handsCounty Auditor
Recording, first two pages$17 base fee plus $17 housing trust fund feeCounty Recorder
Recording, each added page$4 base fee plus $4 housing trust fund feeCounty Recorder
Document preservation surchargeUp to $5, if the county charges itCounty Recorder

Sources: the Fairfield County Auditor's conveyance fact sheet and Ohio Revised Code 317.32. The Recorder's own fee schedule is linked from the Recorder page, so confirm the surcharge and any other line there before you write a check. A county can also levy a real property transfer tax of up to 30 cents per $100 under R.C. 322.02, which the grantor pays to the Auditor before the Recorder sees the deed.

Who can acknowledge a deed in Ohio, and where must it be recorded?

An Ohio deed must be signed by the grantor, and the signing must be acknowledged before an authorized officer (R.C. 5301.01). The statute names these officers:

  • a judge or clerk of a court of record in Ohio
  • a county auditor or county engineer
  • a notary public
  • a mayor

A deed is filed where the land sits. Under R.C. 5301.25, a deed that has not been recorded is treated as fraudulent against a later good faith buyer who had no knowledge of it. For a Fairfield County house, that means the deed belongs on file in Lancaster, whether the home sits in Pickerington, Canal Winchester, Reynoldsburg or an unincorporated township.

The Recorder enters each instrument in the order presented, with the date and exact time. Ohio law (R.C. 317.13) lets the Recorder decline an instrument that is materially false or fraudulent, and a person whose instrument is refused can ask the Court of Common Pleas to order recording.

Can a Fairfield County deed be recorded electronically?

Yes, through Simplifile, which the Auditor's fact sheet names as the electronic filing route. The Auditor adds that a one-time filer may find the process impractical and can use paper instead.

Ohio set a statutory target of June 30, 2026 for every county recorder, auditor and engineer to offer electronic recording of real property conveyances, and for recorders to post electronic indexes and images of instruments recorded since January 1, 1980. That date has passed, and it lines up with the 1980 online start on the Fairfield page. A recorder may require a username and password to view those records but cannot charge for one.

Paper filing still works. Mail or drop off the deed with the Auditor, then send the Recorder its fee. Ask the Recorder's office at 740-652-7100 how to get the original returned to you.

What should a Fairfield County seller know about the county itself?

Fairfield County was founded December 9, 1800, with Lancaster as county seat and largest city. It covers 509 square miles, mostly land, and had 158,921 residents at the 2020 census. The county belongs to the Columbus metropolitan area. Franklin County lies to the northwest, Licking County to the north, Perry County to the east, Hocking County to the south and Pickaway County to the southwest, so a mailing address in a neighboring county does not change where a Fairfield County parcel is recorded.

The northern part is flat and was glaciated, while the land south of U.S. 22 turns hilly toward the Hocking Hills. Buckeye Lake lies partly in the northeast corner. Cities named on the county page include Lancaster, Pickerington, Canal Winchester and Reynoldsburg. Ask the city or township office where the house sits about any open permit before you list.

Because the Auditor, Recorder and Treasurer sit in separate offices, build a short checklist before closing: legal description approved, conveyance fee statement signed, taxes confirmed with the Treasurer, then recording.

  • Legal description cleared by the Auditor's Map Room
  • Deed signed and acknowledged before an authorized officer
  • Statement of value (DTE 100 or DTE 100EX) completed
  • Transfer and conveyance fees paid at the Auditor's transfer desk
  • Recording fee sent to the Recorder

What should I do if I suspect fraud on a Fairfield County property?

Enroll in the Recorder's free alerts first, since they flag new documents filed under your name or a notary's name. Then call the Recorder at 740-652-7100 to ask what was filed, and contact an attorney about next steps.

The Recorder also issues Veteran ID cards, and the office asks callers to phone 740-652-7100 for that service.

More questions about Fairfield County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Which office files a deed for a Fairfield County house?

At the Fairfield County Recorder, 210 East Main Street, Suite 205, Lancaster, after the County Auditor has processed the transfer. The Auditor's office is a separate stop at 108 N. High Street.

What does the Auditor charge to transfer a deed in Fairfield County?

The Auditor's fact sheet lists a $.50 per parcel transfer fee and a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of consideration when money changes hands. Ask the transfer desk to confirm the amount before you bring payment.

Does Fairfield County have its own deed form?

No. The Recorder does not provide forms for recording and staff cannot help prepare a document. A title company or attorney usually drafts the deed, and the Auditor's Map Room reviews the legal description.

Can I look up old Fairfield County deeds from home?

Yes. Indexes go back to 1800 and images are online from January 1980 forward through the Recorder's land records search. Older documents are at the office.

Who pays the conveyance fee when a house sells?

The seller does. Ohio law puts the conveyance fee on the grantor, while the buyer files the statement of value with the Auditor.

Where is the Fayette County Recorder, and what does the office handle?

The Fayette County Recorder is at 133 S. Main Street, Suite 305, in Washington Court House, and is open Monday through Friday from 8 am to 4 pm. Call 740-335-1770 or fax 740-333-3521. The office is responsible for all real estate and personal property records in the county.

The county page lists the kinds of papers the office files:

  • deeds, mortgages and land contracts
  • IRS liens and mechanics liens
  • plats and zoning resolutions
  • military service discharges

Washington Court House is the county seat and the county's only city. Every deed for a Fayette County parcel is recorded at this one office, whether the house is in town or out in a township.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Fayette County?

Fayette County posts a flat price by page count, and the first two pages cost the same. The table repeats the figures printed on the Recorder's page.

Pages in the documentFee printed by the Recorder
1 page$39.00
2 pages$39.00
3 pages$47.00
4 pages$55.00
5 pages$63.00
10 pages$103.00

Source: Fayette County Recorder page. The page adds that a $4.00 marginal fee still applies. The schedule runs page by page up to ten pages, so ask the office for the price of a longer deed. Ohio Revised Code 317.32 sets the structure behind these numbers: a base fee and a housing trust fund fee for each page, plus an optional document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars that the county may keep for its general fund.

How do I deliver a deed to the Fayette County Recorder?

Bring it to Suite 305 or mail it, and pay by cash or check. The Recorder states that credit and debit cards are not accepted.

  • Documents received after 3:30 PM are held and run the next day, so a late afternoon drop does not get that day's time stamp.
  • Anything that must be mailed back needs a self-addressed, stamped envelope included with the papers.
  • Since June 22, 2026, the county offers e-recording through Simplifile for both conveyance and non-conveyance documents.

The time stamp matters because Ohio recorders file instruments in order of presentation and note the exact time (R.C. 317.13). If two papers arrive for the same house, the earlier time gets priority.

What does the Fayette County Auditor do before the deed is recorded?

The Auditor's real estate department tracks deed transfers, new parcels, lot splits and homestead exemptions, and a deed for a sale is presented there before it goes to the Recorder. The Auditor's office is at 133 S. Main Street, Suite 303, with the phone at 740-335-6461 and the same Monday to Friday, 8 am to 4 pm schedule.

The Auditor's forms page carries the conveyance papers: the Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100), the Exemption from Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100EX), a statement for homestead property, a statement for current agricultural use valuation property, and forms for mobile homes. The county also posts its conveyance standards for legal descriptions.

The DTE 100 asks for the total consideration and then the portion paid for items other than real property, and the fee is figured on the real property consideration that remains. It also asks whether the seller said the home receives the senior or disabled homestead exemption or farm use valuation, and whether the buyer will live there by January 1 of the next year. The form itself warns that skipping the owner-occupancy application blocks that 2.5 percent reduction until a proper, timely application is filed, so fill that part in. Ask the Auditor for the county's current conveyance fee rate before closing.

Which papers can a Fayette County Recorder refuse to record?

An Ohio recorder may decline an instrument that is not required or authorized to be recorded, or that the recorder has reasonable cause to believe is materially false or fraudulent. Someone whose paper is turned away can ask the Court of Common Pleas to order recording.

One refusal is mandatory. The recorder must refuse a right-to-list home sale agreement described in R.C. 5301.94. A Fayette County owner who is told such an agreement will be recorded against the house should know the statute directs the recorder to turn it away.

A recorder has no duty to inspect or investigate what is handed over. Checking the legal description, names and signatures is the job of whoever drafted the deed.

What do copies and small extras cost under Ohio law?

R.C. 317.32 sets several charges besides the recording fee, each split into a base fee and a housing trust fund fee of equal size:

  • Certified copy of a recorded document: $1 base plus $1 trust fund per page, with a further 50 cents plus 50 cents when the recorder's seal is required.
  • Photocopy outside the recording process: $1 plus $1 per page.
  • Marginal reference entered by a separate instrument: $2 plus $2 for each reference, which matches the $4.00 marginal fee Fayette posts.
  • Local fax or electronic transmission: $1 plus $1 per page.

For a seller, a certified copy of the vesting deed is the most common extra, and a title company often asks for one.

How do Fayette County values and tax bills connect to a sale?

The Auditor is the county's chief fiscal officer and also its real property appraiser. Ohio directs a general reappraisal every six years, with an update in the third year. Each year the Auditor prepares the tax list, and after the Treasurer collects, the Auditor distributes the money to townships, schools and other taxing bodies. The Auditor also certifies and publishes the list of delinquent taxes, and the Treasurer then pursues those accounts.

The Auditor serves as secretary of the county Board of Revision, and the Board of Revision Property Complaint form is on the Auditor's forms page. A seller who disputes a value uses that form, and does not take the question to the Recorder.

At the deed stage, state law requires the conveyance statement to confirm that the seller was asked whether the home gets a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction, and whether it was in farm use valuation. If farm use ends, a recoupment charge can follow, and buyer and seller are expected to account for it between themselves (R.C. 319.202). A seller of acreage that has been in farm use should raise this with the title agent early.

What should a seller know about Fayette County?

Fayette County was formed on March 1, 1810 from parts of Highland and Ross counties and named for the Marquis de Lafayette. It covers 407 square miles of nearly all land and counted 28,951 residents in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 28,552. The median age was 41.5 years, and 19.2 percent of residents were 65 or older.

The county touches Madison, Pickaway, Ross, Highland, Clinton and Greene counties. Washington Court House anchors a micropolitan area that is part of the Columbus-Marion-Zanesville region. Good Hope and Pancoastburg are the named unincorporated places on the county map. The Tri-County Triangle Trail connects Washington Court House with Chillicothe.

If the Auditor's online data for your parcel looks wrong, the Auditor's page asks owners to report the problem so the record can be corrected.

More questions about Fayette County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How much is the Fayette County recording fee for a two page deed?

$39.00, according to the Recorder's printed schedule, and the $4.00 marginal fee can apply on top. A one page deed is also $39.00, and three pages cost $47.00.

Can I pay the Fayette County Recorder by card?

No. The Recorder accepts cash or check only, and credit and debit cards are not accepted.

Can I e-record a deed in Fayette County?

Yes. As of June 22, 2026, the county offers e-recording through Simplifile for conveyance and non-conveyance documents. Paper filing at Suite 305 remains available.

What time should I get a deed to the Fayette County Recorder?

Before 3:30 PM. Documents received after that hour are held and run the following day.

Does the Fayette County Recorder or Auditor handle the conveyance form?

The Auditor, at Suite 303 of the same building. The Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100) and the exemption form (DTE 100EX) are on the Auditor's forms page, and the Recorder then files the deed.

Franklin County by the numbers

Franklin County ranks 1 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 1,321,635 people in 588,892 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $265,700, the median home value sits 45% above the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Franklin County reports $73,795. Owner-occupancy is 53%, so renters hold about 47% of occupied homes.

Where is the Franklin County Recorder, and what does it record?

The Franklin County Recorder is on the 18th floor of the Franklin County Courthouse, 373 South High Street, Columbus. The phone is (614) 525-3930, and questions can go to recorder@franklincountyohio.gov. The office records, preserves and retrieves real estate, personal property and other records so property interests are safeguarded and easy to find.

The Auditor and the Recorder are different offices in this county. The Auditor handles ownership changes and fees for the transfer, while the Recorder files the deed itself. Plan to visit or mail to both.

What is the order of steps to record a deed in Franklin County?

File with the Auditor first, then the deed reaches the Recorder. The Recorder's own guide spells out the sequence:

  • Prepare a new deed form. A template is available through the County Law Library under real estate forms.
  • Get the legal description from the last deed on file, which the Recorder's website lets you search, and follow the county document standards.
  • Sign the deed in front of a notary.
  • File the deed with the Auditor and pay the Auditor's transfer charges.
  • Include a separate payment for the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards the deed to the Recorder once the transfer is complete.

Paying off a mortgage does not call for a new deed. The lender files a release of mortgage as its own document.

What does recording cost at the Franklin County Recorder?

The Recorder bases its fees on Ohio Revised Code 317.32 and publishes a fee calculator for checking your math. The table gives the rates as the Recorder prints them.

ItemFee
First two pages$34
Each additional page$8
Document that fails standardization requirements$20
Each indexed marginal reference$4
Debit or credit card payment3% convenience fee
No self-addressed stamped envelope supplied$1 document return fee

Source: Franklin County Recorder fee page. Make checks and money orders payable to the Franklin County Recorder, since checks payable to second or third parties are refused. Cards are limited to Discover, Mastercard and Visa. The statute shows where the $34 and $8 figures come from: each is a base fee plus a housing trust fund fee of the same amount.

What does the Franklin County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

The Auditor's transfer and conveyance office handles more than 30,000 property transfers a year. Its fee calculator describes a conveyance fee of $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, made up of $1 per $1,000 set by the State of Ohio and $2 per $1,000 set by the Board of Commissioners. There is also a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax on any transfer that is not exempt. An exempt transfer owes only the $0.50.

When the seller is receiving the homestead exemption at the time of transfer, the county's $2 piece is waived and the conveyance fee drops to $1 per $1,000. You can verify homestead status on the Auditor's property search under the Homestead Credit entry on the parcel summary. Round the sale amount up to the next $100 when you use the calculator.

  • Pay by cash, business check or cashier's check made out to the Franklin County Auditor.
  • Personal checks are not accepted, and the office can give change only on cash.
  • Do not add payments for other county offices to the same check.
  • Transfers must carry the exact amount to be processed.

Questions go to the Transfer and Conveyance Department at 614-525-3253.

Can I e-record a Franklin County deed?

Yes, but only through Simplifile, and mostly for professionals. The Recorder does not run an e-recording platform itself. Private companies, including CSC Global, ePN, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile, send documents in for recording and may add their own charges.

Deeds that transfer real property can be e-recorded through the Auditor, Engineer and Recorder, though only via Simplifile, and they need to come from a title company, bank or similar entity. Individuals may e-record other documents through Simplifile, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. If e-recording is out of reach, mail the deed or bring it to the 18th floor.

The Recorder also accepts documents completed with electronic and online notarization that meet Ohio legislature and Secretary of State requirements.

Who gets the original deed back, and can I redact my address?

The original returns by mail if you enclose a self-addressed, stamped envelope. Without one, the Recorder charges postage or the $1 return fee on its fee page.

Regular filers can open an escrow account at the Recorder with a starting deposit of $100 or more, so they do not bring a check for each filing. Certain public servants whose home addresses are exempt from public record may ask to have the address redacted from documents posted on the Recorder's website, using the Request to Redact Address form and emailing it to the Recorder.

What should be in the packet before I go to the courthouse?

Gather these items so one trip covers the Auditor and the Recorder:

  • The signed, notarized deed with a legal description copied from the prior recorded deed
  • The Auditor's payment: cash, business check or cashier's check for the transfer and conveyance charges
  • A second payment made out to the Franklin County Recorder, so the Auditor can forward the deed
  • A self-addressed, stamped envelope for the original
  • Proof of homestead status if the seller receives the exemption, since it lowers the conveyance fee

The Recorder's fee calculator and the Auditor's transfer calculator both help you total these amounts before you leave home.

What should a seller know about Franklin County itself?

Franklin County was created April 30, 1803, less than two months after Ohio became a state, and was named for Benjamin Franklin. It covers about 544 square miles and had 1,323,807 residents in 2020, which makes it the most populous county in Ohio. Columbus is the county seat and the state capital.

The county touches Delaware, Fairfield, Licking, Madison, Pickaway and Union counties. Interstates 70, 71 and 270 cross it, along with U.S. 23, 33, 40 and 62. Suburbs on the county list include Bexley, Dublin, Gahanna, Grandview Heights, Grove City, Hilliard, New Albany, Upper Arlington, Westerville and Worthington. Ohio State University's main campus, with about 60,000 students, sits in Columbus.

The 2020 census found 540,369 households here and a median age of 34.2 years. Whatever the size of the market, each sale goes through the same paperwork, so a complete packet saves a second trip.

All of these places record deeds at the same courthouse, so a house in Dublin and a house in Whitehall follow the same path through the Auditor and then the Recorder.

More questions about Franklin County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How much does the Franklin County Recorder charge for a deed?

The Recorder lists $34 for the first two pages and $8 for each additional page. A $20 fee applies if the document misses the standardization requirements, and cards carry a 3% convenience fee.

Do I file with the Auditor or the Recorder first in Franklin County?

The Auditor first. After the transfer is complete, the deed goes to the Recorder, and the Auditor forwards it if you included a separate payment for the Recorder.

Does a deed need a notary in Franklin County?

Yes. The Recorder's guide says all transfers must be signed in front of a notary, and electronic or online notarization is accepted when it meets Ohio requirements.

What is the Franklin County conveyance fee?

The Auditor's calculator lists $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, with a $3 minimum and a $0.50 transfer tax. The fee drops to $1 per $1,000 if the seller receives the homestead exemption.

Can an individual e-record a deed in Franklin County?

An individual can use Simplifile for some documents, but an individual's e-recording cannot transfer property. Deeds that transfer property come through a title company, bank or similar entity.
