Fulton County by the numbers

Fulton County has about 42,434 residents and 17,708 housing units in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, number 58 by population among the 63 oh counties we cover. The median owner-occupied home is worth $176,000, 4% below the median of the oh counties covered. Median household income is $72,866, against $69,699 for the middle oh county. Owners live in 81% of occupied homes and renters in 19%. The median home was built in 1970, about 53 years ago.

What does the Fulton County Recorder do?

Fulton County's Recorder is the office that files and indexes every land document in the county, so a buyer can trace ownership and a lender can see what debts sit against a parcel. The county's own Recorder page frames the work as recording, safekeeping and organizing those papers so land can be bought with a clear title.

Fulton County lies west of Toledo and belongs to the Toledo metropolitan area. The state created it in 1850 out of Henry, Lucas and Williams counties. Wauseon grew up around a railroad stop in 1854, took the county seat from Ottokee in 1871, and its courthouse went up in 1872. A deed for a house in Archbold, Delta, Swanton, Fayette, Lyons or Metamora is filed in Wauseon as well.

Where do I find the Fulton County Recorder in Wauseon?

Go to 152 S. Fulton St., Suite 175, Wauseon, OH 43567. The staff directory shows weekday service from half past eight to half past four, and the telephone is (419) 337-9232.

  • Recorder: Suite 175, the last stop for a deed.
  • Auditor: Suite 165 in the same building, the first stop. Its real estate line is (419) 337-9200.
  • Land records search: reached from the county's Records Search page, for looking up earlier deeds and mortgages.

The Recorder page also carries a Real Property Conveyance Standards PDF plus printable plats and land surveys. Read them before you draft a legal description.

What steps come before a Fulton County deed reaches the Recorder?

Fulton County's conveyance standards exist to give every legal description a uniform check, correct visible errors and describe the parcel properly for tax purposes. Odd cases go to a panel of the County Engineer, the Auditor and the Planning Director.

  1. Write the deed so its legal description follows the last deed of record.
  2. Sign before a notary. Under R.C. 5301.01 a judge, court clerk, county auditor, county engineer or mayor can also take the acknowledgment.
  3. Take the deed to Suite 165 for the description check, the conveyance fee and the transfer.
  4. Carry it to Suite 175 and pay the recording fee.

Ohio's transfer tax statute has the grantor settle with the Auditor before the deed is handed to the Recorder, so keep this order. Ask the Recorder which endorsement it expects to see.

What does the Fulton County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

The Auditor's price list reads $4.00 per thousand dollars of total consideration, rounded up to the nearest $100, and $0.50 per parcel as a transfer fee. Its own worked example treats $100,001 as $100,100 and arrives at $400.40.

State law builds that number in layers. R.C. 319.54(G)(3) sets a statement-of-value fee of ten cents per $100, and R.C. 322.02 lets a county add as much as thirty cents per $100. The grantor pays on delivery of the deed.

Some transfers carry no fee at all under R.C. 319.54(G)(3), including:

  • gifts between spouses, or from a parent to a child;
  • a transfer where no money or other valuable consideration is paid and the deal is no gift;
  • conveyances among the heirs or devisees of one decedent for no money;
  • a trustee handing property back to the grantor of a revocable trust.

If your sale resembles one of these, ask the Auditor's real estate office before you assume a fee is due.

What will recording a Fulton County deed cost?

The state sets the recording fees, and half of each goes to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. Every printed side counts as a page. Counties may tack on a preservation surcharge, capped at $5.00 per document, so phone the Fulton Recorder for the final figure before mailing a check.

Common charges on a Fulton County deed. Sources: Ohio County Recorders' Association fee schedule; R.C. 317.114; Fulton County Auditor.

What formatting rules does Fulton County enforce on a deed?

R.C. 317.114 sets a standard layout for any deed you hand the Recorder. A deed that misses it is still taken but carries an added $10 base fee and $10 housing trust fee.

  • Type no smaller than ten point.
  • Sheets no smaller than letter size and no longer than 14 inches.
  • Ink in black or blue, nothing highlighted.
  • One inch of white space down both sides and along the foot of each page.
  • Three inches of white space across the head of page one, which the Engineer, Auditor and Recorder use for their endorsements, and one and a half inches on following pages.

The rule skips court and tax-authority papers, plats, state and federal documents, and anything signed before July 1, 2009.

How big and how stable is the Fulton County housing market?

The Census Bureau recorded 42,713 residents in April 2020 and put the July 2025 estimate at 41,853, down 2.0 percent. Owners occupy 80.2 percent of the housing, the median owner-occupied unit is worth $191,000, and the county gave out 57 building permits during 2025. Median household income stands at $72,864.

The county spreads across 405 square miles of land at roughly 105 residents per square mile. Parcels range from farm acreage to village lots in Archbold and Wauseon to homes in any of its twelve townships, Amboy and Chesterfield through Swan Creek and York.

What else shows up in Fulton County's land records during a sale?

A title search in Wauseon covers more than the last deed. The Sheriff's Office explains in its own FAQ that when a house is sold at a sheriff's sale, liens are paid in order from the proceeds and then cancelled against the property, except a federal lien, which stays on file at the Recorder. Buyers at those sales are told to check every lien themselves.

  • Mortgages, releases and assignments are filed in the same office as the deed.
  • Federal tax liens are filed with the Recorder at a $5.00 fee, and releases cost $3.00.
  • Military discharge papers are recorded without a charge.
  • Plats and condominium drawings are priced at ten cents per square inch with a $40.00 minimum.

Search the parcel in the Recorder's land records and the Auditor's property search before you agree on a closing date.

Which Fulton County tax rules should a home seller check?

Fulton County real estate tax bills fall due in February and July. According to the Auditor, the lien date is January 1 and Ohio taxes run one year in arrears: the bill paid in 2025 was for tax year 2024 and was figured on what the home was worth when 2025 began.

  • Owner-occupied reduction: residences only, and it is never applied on its own. Call (419) 337-9200 to enroll.
  • Value complaints: go to the Board of Revision in the window from the first of January to the last day of March.
  • Payments and tax-mailing address changes: the Treasurer handles both, not the Auditor.

Request a payoff figure for the parcel from the Fulton County Treasurer, and have the title company explain who covers each bill.

More questions about Fulton County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Is there a transfer tax collected by the Fulton County Recorder?

The Recorder takes the recording fee only. The conveyance fee of $4.00 per $1,000 and the $0.50 per parcel transfer fee belong to the Auditor, and Ohio law has the grantor pay the Auditor ahead of the filing.

Can a Fulton County deed skip the Auditor and go straight to recording?

Plan on visiting the Auditor first. R.C. 322.02 has the grantor pay the county Auditor before the deed is presented to the Recorder, and the county's conveyance standards put each legal description through a check.

What hours does the Wauseon Recorder keep?

Weekdays, half past eight to half past four, at Suite 175, 152 S. Fulton St. The phone is (419) 337-9232. The Auditor is in Suite 165 of the same building.

What happens if my deed has a small font or thin margins?

The Recorder still files it, but under R.C. 317.114 the bill rises by $10 in base fee and $10 in housing trust fee. Court papers, plats, state and federal documents and instruments signed before July 1, 2009 are excluded.

Where do I send a complaint that my Fulton County home is overvalued?

Address it to the Board of Revision through the Auditor's real estate office at (419) 337-9200. The filing window runs from January 1 to March 31, and the Auditor's staff can mail a form or point you to the printable copy.

  • Recording fees are determined by the State of Ohio per ORC: 50% basic recording fee, 50% to Ohio Housing Trust Fund; 'Table of Fees' on site.

What we could not confirm

Who records deeds in Gallia County, Ohio?

The Gallia County Recorder in Gallipolis records deeds, mortgages, leases, land contracts, liens and plats for the county. The office's own history page says Ohio's first legislature had judges appoint a recorder in each county, the post became elective in 1829, and the term was fixed at four years in 1936.

Gallia County dates to March 25, 1803, and runs along the Ohio River where Ohio meets West Virginia. French settlers gave it the name, and Welsh families arrived in 1818. Gallipolis is the seat, with Cheshire, Crown City, Rio Grande, Centerville and Vinton as the other villages, and every one of them files into the same land records. Part of the Wayne National Forest sits inside the county line.

Where is the Gallia County Recorder's office and what are its hours?

The Recorder is at 18 Locust Street, Gallipolis, Ohio 45631. Weekday hours run eight to four. Call 740-446-4612 and ask for extension 1247, 1248 or 1329.

  • County Auditor: same address, Room 1264, with the real estate desk on extension 1201.
  • Recorder's property search: an online index of recorded documents.
  • Auditor's parcel search, GIS parcel viewer, sales reports and delinquency reports: available from the Auditor's website.

The Recorder does not charge to look at the land records. Its home page says public access to records is at no cost.

What comes first in Gallia County: the Auditor or the Recorder?

The Auditor comes first. The Recorder's requirements for deeds say plainly that a deed must be transferred in the Auditor's office before it is recorded.

On its website the Auditor posts a conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator under Tools, with the statement of value form for the conveyance fee among its forms. The statewide piece of the conveyance fee is a dollar, or ten cents per hundred dollars of value if that is larger (R.C. 319.54(G)(3)). A county board may stack a tax of up to thirty cents per hundred on top (R.C. 322.02). Use the Auditor's calculator for Gallia County's total, and ask the real estate desk about exemptions such as a transfer with no money or other consideration.

The Auditor's office also reports that Gallia County has more than 29,000 parcels and more than 2,500 manufactured and mobile homes, and its website announces a Community Reinvestment Area that began on December 2, 2024. Ask the Auditor what that program covers for your parcel.

What does the Gallia County Recorder require on a deed?

The Recorder publishes a checklist, and a deed or mortgage that misses an item comes back. The list includes:

  • a full legal description naming the township or city, lot or subdivision and acreage;
  • grantor names spelled exactly as they are signed and notarized;
  • the permanent parcel number wherever the real estate is described;
  • a notary signature, seal and expiration date;
  • a "prepared by" line, which Ohio requires;
  • names typed beneath the original signatures;
  • a stamped, addressed return envelope big enough to hold the papers.

The office also warns that its deputies cannot fix a lot number or other typo. Whoever made the document must make the change. Documents boxed for pickup must be claimed within a week or they are mailed out at the box holder's cost.

How much does the Gallia County Recorder charge?

State rules put a deed at $34 for pages one and two and $8 for every later page, with an optional county preservation surcharge of up to $5. Gallia posts $39.00 for the opening two pages and $8.00 for each later page. The state splits each of its fees evenly with the Ohio Housing Trust Fund.

Selected Gallia County Recorder charges. Source: Gallia County Recorder fees page; R.C. 317.114.

What format rules can add $20 to a Gallia County recording?

Ohio's standardization statute, R.C. 317.114, took effect on July 1, 2009. The statute calls for type of ten points or larger, black or blue ink, no highlighting and paper between letter size and 14 inches long. Leave an inch of white space on the sides and the bottom, three inches at the head of the first page and an inch and a half at the head of later ones.

The Recorder will still accept a deed that does not conform, but adds $20.00 to the bill. The statute exempts court and tax authority documents, plats, DD-214 discharges, state and federal papers and anything executed before the effective date. Marginal clutter such as page numbers, initials and bar codes is not charged.

Which other Gallia County records show up in a sale?

Title work on a Gallia County house often turns up more than the deed. The Recorder's fee page lists the other filings that sit in the same indexes.

  • Mechanic's liens and notices of commencement.
  • Federal tax liens and releases, personal property tax liens and workers' compensation liens.
  • Land contracts, powers of attorney and trust documents.
  • A Notice to Medicaid Estate Recovery of Pending Transfer of Property, a form the Recorder links on its fees page.

Run the parcel through the Recorder's search and the Auditor's search before you sign a contract. A lien found after a contract is signed holds up the closing.

What does Census data say about Gallia County housing?

The 2020 count for Gallia was 29,220 people, and the July 2025 estimate is 29,072. Three of every four homes are owner-held (74.7 percent), their median value is $155,600, and the county's median rent is $813 against a median household income of $56,830.

Gallia's land area is about 467 square miles, and the 2020 Census found 13.1 percent of the 13,430 housing units vacant. Only seven building permits were issued in 2025. A seller here is often handling an older house in a county where new construction is thin, which makes the title and lien check even more worth doing.

Gallipolis is the county seat and largest village, and the county is part of the Point Pleasant, West Virginia and Ohio micropolitan area, with Cabell and Mason counties across the river. Bring that in when you talk to a buyer from across the state line: the deed still records in Gallipolis, and the Auditor's records and the Recorder's records are the two places to check first.

More questions about Gallia County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the first-two-pages recording fee in Gallia County?

The Recorder's fee page lists $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after them. The state base is $34, which a county may raise with a preservation surcharge of up to $5.

Which Gallipolis office comes first, the Auditor or the Recorder?

Yes. Per the Recorder's own deed requirements, the transfer in the Auditor's office has to happen before recording. Both offices are at 18 Locust Street, and the Auditor's real estate desk is on extension 1201.

Can the Recorder correct an error in my legal description?

No. The office says deputies cannot change lot numbers or other details even when the error looks like a typo. The person who prepared the document has to fix it and sign again.

Is there a charge to record a veteran's discharge in Gallia County?

No. The Recorder records discharge papers and the Honorable Discharge Certificate at no cost, and the fees page lists one certified copy of a service discharge as free.

How do I look up an old Gallia County deed?

Use the Recorder's online records index, or the Auditor's parcel search by owner, parcel or address. The counter at 18 Locust Street runs on weekday hours, eight to four, and browsing the records costs nothing.

Who records deeds in Geauga County

  • Geauga County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

Fees

Selling in Geauga County?
We buy Geauga County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What we could not confirm

  • Millage not retrieved (auditor tax-info page references 2023 rates table)

Geauga County by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts 95,479 people and 37,617 housing units in Geauga County, which ranks 29 of 63 oh counties here. Median home value is $305,100, which is 67% above the middle county in this oh set. Households here earn a median $100,783; the middle oh county is at $69,699. 13% of occupied homes are rented, which leaves 87% owner-occupied.

How does a deed get recorded in Geauga County?

A Geauga County deed passes through three offices in Chardon, and the county publishes a one-page reference sheet effective June 30, 2026 that lays out the order. First the Engineer approves the legal description. Next the Auditor transfers the parcel and takes the conveyance fee. Last, the Recorder files the deed and sends it back.

Geauga sits in Ohio's northeast corner inside the Cleveland metropolitan area, with Chardon as its seat. The county was founded on March 1, 1806, as the second county in the Connecticut Western Reserve, and its first settlement was at Burton in 1798.

What does each of the three Chardon offices handle?

The reference sheet lists the three stops, their addresses and what each one needs from you.

  • County Engineer, 12665 Merritt Rd, Chardon, phone (440) 279-1800: reviews the legal description and stamps it with an original (wet) stamp. No fee. Allow 2 to 3 business days. Bring a legible copy of the prior deed with its volume and page reference.
  • County Auditor, 231 Main St, Suite 1-A, phone (440) 279-1600: transfers the property and updates the tax records. Needs the original signed and notarized deed.
  • County Recorder, 231 Main St, Suite 1-C, phone (440) 279-2020: records the deed and mails the original back.

The Recorder's page puts the Auditor two doors down the hall. To send a deed by mail, enclose a brief letter saying what you want done, your phone number, a stamped return envelope and two separate checks, payable to the Recorder and to the Auditor.

What does the Geauga County Auditor charge to transfer a deed?

The Auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of transfer value and $0.50 per parcel, and checks for both are made payable to the Geauga County Auditor. The Recorder's FAQ also puts the conveyance fee at four dollars per thousand and refers fee questions to the Auditor.

Ohio law explains the split. The first layer is the statement-of-value fee in R.C. 319.54(G)(3), ten cents on each hundred dollars. The second is a county tax capped at thirty cents per hundred under R.C. 322.02, which the grantor pays to the Auditor ahead of recording. The statute exempts some transfers, among them spousal and parent-to-child gifts, deals with no consideration and certain trust moves.

The Recorder asks for a completed DTE 100 or DTE 100EX conveyance form with the deed. A Transfer on Death Affidavit is the exception the Recorder names: it has no Auditor fee.

How much does the Geauga County Recorder charge?

State law fixes the Recorder's charge at $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page that follows. A check that is short or too large gets the document returned unrecorded, so count pages before writing it.

Geauga County recording and transfer charges. Sources: Geauga County Recorder transfer reference sheet (effective June 30, 2026); Recorder FAQs.

Can I record a Geauga County deed electronically?

The reference sheet says electronic recording of conveyances is available and lets you skip the paper steps, and the 2026 sheet also says legal descriptions presented that way do not need the wet Engineer stamp. An older Recorder page still says eRecording is not available for any document that needs conveyance through the Auditor, so call (440) 279-2020 to confirm what the office will take.

Paper filings are on a fast clock. The Recorder's FAQ gives same-day turnaround, and an electronic recording is returned when it is recorded. Leave a self-addressed stamped envelope with an in-person deed, or come back the next day to pick it up.

What are the Geauga County Recorder's document rules?

The sheet lists what each deed needs before it reaches the counter.

  • Legible signatures, and printed names under any that are hard to read.
  • A line naming whoever prepared the deed.
  • Notary acknowledgments for each grantor.
  • Original wet stamps from the Engineer and the Auditor.
  • The 8-digit permanent parcel numbers.
  • A completed conveyance form.

The extra $20 for a non-standard document comes from R.C. 317.114, which wants at least ten point type, black or blue ink and three blank inches above the text on page one. Staff cannot notarize or give legal advice, and state law keeps them from running title searches. The Recorder stopped accepting Torrens registered land filings, and it does not sell blank forms.

What else does the Geauga County Recorder keep for owners and sellers?

The Recorder's FAQ covers several points that arise around a sale. Geauga County has no tract (geographical) indexing, and only the indexes of recorded documents are online, so a full copy of an old deed means a copy request. Copies made by the public cost ten cents a page, while a copy made with staff help is two dollars a page.

  • Releases and assignments do not need a legal description, but they do carry the $4.00 marginal notation fee.
  • Soldier discharge records (DD214) are recorded, and a recorded discharge is what the office uses to issue a Veterans ID card.
  • Blank forms are not sold. For one, the FAQ points you to a title company, an attorney or an office supply store.
  • The office will not search the title for you, and it will not notarize or give legal advice.

A shortage or overage on the check sends the document back unrecorded, so call (440) 279-2020 with the page count if you are unsure. The mailing address and the delivery address are the same, 231 Main Street, Suite 1-C, so a courier and the postal service reach one door.

What do Geauga County's housing numbers look like to a seller?

The 2020 Census put Geauga's population at 95,397, and the July 2025 estimate is 95,676. Owner-occupancy is 87.2 percent, the middle-of-the-road owned home is valued at $331,100, and household income has a median of $107,860. Builders pulled 180 permits there in 2025.

Streams that feed the Cuyahoga, Chagrin and Grand rivers start in this county's 400 square miles of land. An average year brings more than 42 inches of precipitation to most of it, more than any other northern Ohio county, so drainage and basements deserve attention before you list.

Chardon, Burton, Middlefield, South Russell and Hunting Valley are the municipalities, and the townships include Bainbridge, Munson, Russell and Newbury. In November 2024 voters dissolved the Village of Aquilla, and a transition board oversees the change.

More questions about Geauga County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What are the total charges to record a deed in Geauga County?

At the Recorder, plan on $34.00 for two pages, $8.00 for each extra one and $20.00 more for a non-standard deed. The Auditor bills $4.00 per $1,000 of value and $0.50 per parcel on its own.

Do I need the County Engineer for a Geauga County deed?

Yes, for paper filings. The Engineer reviews and approves the legal description with an original stamp at no fee, usually within 2 to 3 business days. Legal descriptions sent through electronic recording are the exception.

Where is the Geauga County Recorder located?

Find it at 231 Main Street, Suite 1-C, Chardon, Ohio 44024, or ring (440) 279-2020. The County Auditor is in Suite 1-A of the same building.

Will the Recorder search the title to my house?

No. The Recorder's FAQ says state law prohibits the office from doing title searches. Try the online index of recorded documents, or hire a title company or an attorney.

How long does recording take in Chardon?

The Recorder lists a same-day turnaround. Mailed deeds come back to you after recording in the self-addressed stamped envelope you include, and an electronic recording is returned when it is recorded.

Greene County by the numbers

Greene County has about 168,531 residents and 71,925 housing units in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, number 18 by population among the 63 oh counties we cover. The median owner-occupied home is worth $238,000, 30% above the median of the oh counties covered. Median household income is $85,218, against $69,699 for the middle oh county. Owners live in 68% of occupied homes and renters in 32%.

Where does the Greene County Recorder work, and until when?

Find the office on the third floor of 69 Greene St. in Xenia. The recorder's page posts two sets of hours on weekdays: the counter is staffed until 4:00 p.m., while recording itself stops at 3:00 p.m. After that, expect a deed to sit until the following business day.

Permanent land records for the whole county live here. The published list of filings is long, and a seller will touch several of these during a sale:

  • Deeds, mortgages and releases of mortgage
  • Easements, leases and land contracts
  • Affidavits, trusts and powers of attorney
  • Mechanic's liens, federal tax liens and child support liens
  • Plats, condominium documents and annexations

The office also files and certifies military discharges. Those are closed to the public, and the veteran or heirs can ask for a copy free of charge.

What has to happen before a Greene County deed is recorded?

Stop at the auditor first. The transfer page there asks for a finished Statement of Value (DTE 100) or the exempt version (DTE 100 EX), fees payable to the auditor, a grantor name spelled as in the grantor's own deed, and map department initials. The grantor signs, and a notary acknowledges the signature.

R.C. 5301.01 names the officials who may take that acknowledgment, from notaries and mayors to court clerks, auditors and engineers. Recording protects the buyer as well. Under R.C. 5301.25, a deed left unrecorded counts as fraudulent toward a later purchaser who bought in good faith without notice of it.

Land in the CAUV farm program, in the filing year or the year before, needs that program's conveyance statement attached. If a survey was made, the deed has to carry the surveyor's name.

What will recording a deed cost in Greene County?

R.C. 317.32 sets the schedule, and every charge pairs a base amount with a matching housing trust fund amount. Senate Bill 94 opened the door to as much as $5.00 more per document, yet a January 2, 2026 notice from the Greene County Recorder says standard fees stay unchanged.

Recording fees printed in R.C. 317.32 (base plus housing trust fund)
ItemBase feeHousing trust fund fee
Record and index, first two pages$17$17
Each added page$4$4
Marginal reference by separate instrument$2$2
Certified copy, per page$1$1
Document preservation surchargeUp to $5None listed

Copies are cheaper when you make them yourself: $.10 a page for self-service official copies versus $2.00 a page when staff do it.

Which transfer charges come before recording in Greene County?

The auditor collects these. On its page the county shows a combined $2.00 per thousand dollars of purchase price, built from a $1.00 conveyance fee plus a $1.00 transfer fee, along with $0.50 per parcel. An online calculator is posted.

The grantor owes the tax, and R.C. 322.02 caps a county's own transfer tax at 30 cents per hundred dollars of value. Some transfers carry no fee under R.C. 319.54, including these:

  • Moves among heirs or devisees of one decedent where no money is paid
  • Gifts between spouses or from parent to child
  • Deeds into a revocable trust, and back out to the grantor
  • Deeds given only to secure or release a debt

The reason for the exemption goes on the statement, so review it with the closing agent.

Which liens can show up against a Greene County seller?

The recorder's published list names the liens it files, and a buyer's title company will search for each one against the seller's name and the parcel. Liens on the county's list include mechanic's liens, Medicaid fraud liens, federal tax liens, child support liens, unemployment compensation liens, personal tax liens and workers' compensation liens. A Notice of Commencement is filed here as well.

The Ohio Recorders' Association table gives the fee for several of them, and the amounts differ by type:

  • Federal tax lien (IRS): $5.00, with $3.00 to release it.
  • Unemployment compensation lien and workers' compensation lien: no fee.
  • Personal property tax lien and Medicaid fraud lien: no fee.
  • Mechanic's lien and its release: the standard per-page fee.

A seller who knows of a lien should ask the lienholder for a recorded release before closing day. Once the release is filed, it appears in the same index as the original lien, which lets the title examiner clear the exception.

Which deed forms turn up in Greene County sales?

The state fee table names the usual choices, each recorded at the same per-page rates: warranty, limited warranty, quit claim and survivorship deeds. Estate and trust sales bring executor's, administrator's, guardian's or trustee's deeds, according to who holds authority. A transfer on death designation affidavit appears too.

Survivorship deeds fall under R.C. 5302.20: language showing clear intent creates the tenancy, and a conveyance from every tenant ends it. Co-owners who inherited together should read the recorded deed to see whether they hold in survivorship or in common.

Which communities record deeds in Xenia?

Land is recorded where it sits, so parcels in every city, village and township here go through the Xenia office. Beavercreek, Bellbrook, Fairborn and Xenia are the cities, and Kettering extends into Greene County although most of it is in Montgomery County. The county takes its name from Revolutionary War General Nathanael Greene, and Clark, Madison, Fayette, Clinton, Warren and Montgomery counties touch its borders.

Highways include I-675, I-71, US 35, US 42 and US 68. With more than 73,000 parcels on the auditor's rolls, each parcel has its own chain of recorded documents, and a buyer's title search reads that chain back through earlier deeds. A gap in it can slow a sale.

Public districts here are Beavercreek, Bellbrook-Sugarcreek, Cedar Cliff, Fairborn, Greeneview, Xenia Community and Yellow Springs.

How do you search records and find a mortgage release in Greene County?

Online, the Recorder's Document Search covers filings from 1984 onward. Website images carry a watermark, and a watermarked page cannot be submitted for recording, so pull clean copies at the counter. A transfer tracking table reports where a newly submitted transfer stands, and a fraud alert service can notify an owner when something is filed against a registered property.

A lender gets 90 days after payoff to file the release or satisfaction of mortgage. An owner who cleared a loan long ago should look up that release before listing, since a missing one can stall a closing.

What household numbers does the Census give for Greene County?

Greene County had 68,166 households in the 2020 to 2024 survey, averaging 2.38 people, and roughly 74,000 housing units in 2025. Monthly owner costs have a median of $1,702 with a mortgage and $700 without one. Builders pulled 567 permits in 2025, and 92.8 percent of households subscribe to broadband, which helps with online document submissions.

More questions about Greene County, OH Recorder of Deeds

When does Greene County stop recording documents each day?

At 3:00 p.m. on weekdays, with recording starting at 7:30 a.m. The office itself stays open until 4:00 p.m., so bring anything urgent early in the day.

Did Greene County raise recording fees after the state change?

Not for standard documents. A January 2, 2026 recorder notice says fees stay put, although Senate Bill 94 permits up to $5.00 more.

Which office collects the Greene County transfer charge?

The auditor, from the grantor, ahead of recording. Its page lists $2.00 per thousand dollars of price and a $0.50 per-parcel charge.

How do I get a copy of my Greene County deed?

Go to 69 Greene St., third floor, or use the online document search. Self-service official copies cost $.10 a page, and staff-made ones cost $2.00 a page.

How soon must a lender record a mortgage release in Greene County?

Within ninety days of payoff. The recorder holds the release, and copies come from the counter or the document search.

The Guernsey County recorder of deeds records Ohio deeds and mortgages.

Who records deeds in Guernsey County

  • Guernsey County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

Fees

Selling in Guernsey County?
We buy Guernsey County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What we could not confirm

  • Fee schedule amounts not retrieved

How can sellers contact the Guernsey County Recorder?

Per the county recorder page, the office opens at 8 a.m. and closes at 4 p.m. on weekdays. Call 740-432-9275, or send a fax to 740-439-6267. Cambridge is the county seat and largest city, and the auditor works from the Administration Building at 627 Wheeling Avenue.

Ohio recorders hold the ownership record for land and each lien against it. A seller whose own deed was never recorded should expect the buyer's title company to pause the sale until that gap is closed.

Does Guernsey County take electronic deeds?

Yes. Four submitting vendors can send eRecordings to the recorder, a route used mostly by lenders, banks, attorneys and title companies. Only document types that the office takes by regular mail qualify, and each vendor sets its own price.

A second route, described on the auditor's page, is e-filing through Kofile Technologies. Transmission is open every hour of every day, but staff process files only between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. on weekdays, so a late upload waits a business day. Plats and military discharges (DD-214) cannot go this way. When a deed or conveyance form is rejected, processing restarts once the corrected version arrives.

What happens at the Guernsey County Auditor before recording?

Real estate staff there move the deed onto the tax records and then pass it to the recorder. Its suite is 301 at 627 Wheeling Avenue, and the phone is (740) 432-9243, option 1 for real estate. Forms for sellers and closing agents include:

  • DTE 100, the real estate conveyance form, and DTE 100 EX for exempt transfers
  • DTE 101, the statement of conveyance of homestead property
  • DTE 102, the statement of conveyance of CAUV property
  • A routing sheet and a timeline for deed transfers
  • Transfer and Conveyance Standards effective October 1, 2022

A conveyance fee calculator sits under tools on the auditor's site. State fees come from R.C. 319.54 ($1.00 per thousand) and R.C. 322.02 (a county transfer tax of up to 30 cents per hundred dollars), so rely on the calculator or a phone call for the Guernsey County total.

What does the conveyance statement ask in Guernsey County?

R.C. 319.202 governs the form. A buyer or the buyer's representative files it ahead of the auditor's endorsement. It declares the property's value, meaning the whole price with any mortgage or vendor's lien included, and willfully falsifying that figure is prohibited.

The same statute adds questions on tax reductions and farm status:

  • Either an affirmation that the seller was asked about a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the current or prior year's taxes, or a sworn statement giving the reduction and its estimated amount.
  • Either an affirmation about current agricultural use valuation (CAUV) status, or a sworn statement noting a possible recoupment charge.
  • The reason for any exemption, written on the form when no fee is due.

After endorsement the auditor retains the original, sends a copy to the tax commissioner and hands one to the buyer. Residential rental property gets an added notice telling the buyer to register with the auditor.

What fees apply at the Guernsey County Recorder?

Charges track R.C. 317.32. Combined, the Ohio Recorders' Association table reads $34.00 for the opening two pages, $8.00 per page after that and $4.00 per marginal notation, with up to $5.00 per document for preservation. Half of every fee funds basic recording and the other half the state's Housing Trust Fund.

The table also lists a $10.00 plus $10.00 standardization fee for a document that misses the formatting rules. Ask the recorder at 740-432-9275 whether Guernsey County adds the surcharge, because that choice rests with each county.

Who can notarize a deed signed in Guernsey County?

After the grantor signs, someone from the list in R.C. 5301.01 has to witness the acknowledgment. That list takes in notaries, mayors, the auditor, the engineer, and judges or court clerks. Banks, title companies and law offices usually keep a notary on staff.

R.C. 5301.25 sends each deed to the county of the land and labels an unrecorded one fraudulent as against a later buyer acting in good faith. A deed made after a survey must carry the surveyor's name.

How does a homestead reduction affect a Guernsey County sale?

The auditor's information page explains the homestead rules that sit behind the statement questions above. A homeowner qualifies by owning and occupying the home as a principal residence on January 1 of the year of application, and by meeting one of three tests: age 65 by December 31 of the filing year, total and permanent disability, or being the surviving spouse of a past recipient who was at least 59. Owners with more than one home count as living where they are registered to vote and where their federal income tax form places them.

Ohio returned to income testing in 2013, but anyone who received the credit for tax year 2013 keeps it without an income limit. Disabled veterans with a qualifying federal rating receive a reduction equal to the tax on $50,000 of true value, compared with $25,000 for the standard credit, and the spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty receives the same $50,000 level with no income limit.

Which Guernsey County office handles which step?

Offices on a Guernsey County sale and the contacts the county publishes
StepOfficePublished contact
Moving the deed on tax records, conveyance formCounty Auditor(740) 432-9243, option 1
Filing the deed in the land recordsCounty Recorder740-432-9275
Electronic filing questionsAuditor and RecorderKofile e-filing, 24 hours a day
Delinquent tax listCounty AuditorNotice on the auditor's home page

The auditor's delinquent tax notice cites R.C. 5721.03 and warns that listed parcels will be certified for foreclosure or a tax certificate sale unless every delinquent tax, assessment, interest and penalty is paid within a year. If the seller's parcel is on the list, pay it at or before closing.

What does Census data show for Guernsey County owners?

Guernsey County lies in the Appalachian foothills, organized in 1810, with about 522 square miles of land, and the auditor counts 40,170 parcels. Census estimates give 38,379 residents in 2025, about level with 2020, and 22.1 percent are 65 or older.

Owners hold 72.1 percent of homes, with a $157,700 median in the 2020 to 2024 survey, while renters pay a $864 median gross rent. Median household income is $58,478, and 41 building permits were issued in 2025. The auditor's forms list includes a Mineral Deeds section, so ask the buyer's title company to search for any recorded mineral deed or lease on the parcel.

How large are Guernsey County households and neighborhoods?

There are 16,318 households averaging 2.31 people, and 19,116 housing units as of 2025. Monthly owner costs have a median of $1,237 with a mortgage and $505 without one. Broadband reaches 86.4 percent of households.

Density is 73.6 people per square mile, and the average commute takes 22.9 minutes. Four townships passed to Noble County in 1851, and the county borders Tuscarawas, Coshocton, Harrison, Noble, Muskingum and Belmont counties. Buffalo, Kimbolton and Salesville are census-designated places outside Cambridge, and deeds for land there are recorded in the same Cambridge office.

More questions about Guernsey County, OH Recorder of Deeds

When is the Guernsey County Recorder open?

Weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. Call 740-432-9275, and note that electronic filings get processed only until 3 p.m.

Can a deed be eRecorded in Guernsey County?

Yes, through one of four submitting vendors or through Kofile e-filing. Plats and military discharges are excluded, and a title company usually handles the upload.

Does the deed go to the auditor or the recorder first?

The auditor, who transfers it on the tax records with a conveyance form and then forwards it to the recorder. The auditor posts a timeline for deed transfers.

What is the basic recording charge in Guernsey County?

The Ohio Recorders' Association table shows $34.00 for two pages plus $8.00 for each more page, and up to $5.00 as a preservation surcharge. Check with the recorder about any county surcharge.

What is the risk of leaving a deed unrecorded?

R.C. 5301.25 treats it as fraudulent against a later buyer who acted in good faith without notice. Record it as soon as the auditor has transferred it.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326

The Hamilton County recorder of deeds records Ohio deeds and mortgages.

Who records deeds in Hamilton County

  • Hamilton County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

Fees

Selling in Hamilton County?
We buy Hamilton County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Hamilton County by the numbers

Hamilton County ranks 3 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 827,878 people in 380,414 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $225,700, the median home value sits 23% above the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Hamilton County reports $70,816. Owner-occupancy is 59%, so renters hold about 41% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1963, about 60 years ago.

Where do I take a deed to be recorded in Hamilton County?

Go to Room 205 at 138 East Court Street in Cincinnati. The office admits the public from 7:30 AM until 4:00 PM on weekdays, though the desk that accepts new filings shuts at 3:30 PM.

Mail goes to the same room. Include a stamped envelope bearing your own address, and expect the office to return the recorded deed in about two or three business days. Blank forms are not sold there, so a deed has to come from a lawyer, a closing agent or your own drafting.

Staff are not permitted to search records for customers. Anyone who needs title work should hire an examiner. Employees will gladly teach you the online index, and both the index and the document images cost nothing to view.

How big is Hamilton County, and who owns homes there?

Hamilton County fills the southwest corner of Ohio, with Cincinnati as its seat. After the 2020 count it ranked third in population among Ohio counties. Of its 413 square miles, about 406 are land, folded into hills where the Great Miami, the Little Miami and Mill Creek meet the Ohio River valley.

Territorial officials created the county in 1790, the second in the Northwest Territory, and that early start explains why the Recorder's site can display scanned deed books from 1794 onward.

  • Headcount: 838,418 by the July 2025 estimate, against 830,639 counted in 2020.
  • Housing stock: 383,689 units, with 59.3% of households owning.
  • Homeowners report a median home value of $241,900 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,075, and the county logged 1,162 building permits for 2025.

Figures from QuickFacts for Hamilton County, with geography and history from the county's Wikipedia entry.

Which Hamilton County office sees a deed first?

The Auditor comes first and the Recorder second. By mail, the Recorder takes a conveyance only with the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps already on it, and staff will not carry the deed through those stops on your behalf.

  1. Have the deed drafted, signed and acknowledged.
  2. Fill out the conveyance form: DTE Form 100 when value is declared, DTE Form 100 EX when an exemption applies.
  3. Bring the deed, forms and fee to Room 304, the Auditor's Transfer Desk, on the same street.
  4. Take the stamped deed to Room 205, adding a return envelope if you want it mailed back.

The Transfer Desk keeps the same weekday hours, but paperwork arriving after 3:20 PM is held until the next business day. Because that cutoff comes before the Recorder's 3:30 PM close, leave time for the Auditor stop in the morning.

What are the recording fees at the Hamilton County Recorder?

Two pages of a deed, mortgage, lease or power of attorney cost $34.00 together, with $8.00 for every further page. The office adds that the Ohio General Assembly, and not the county, sets these amounts.

ServiceAmount listed
First two pages$34.00 (minimum fee $34.00)
Each added page$8.00
Certified copy$2.00 a page plus a $1.00 seal
Self-serve copy$0.10 a page
Copy made by staff$2.00 a page
Marginal notation on a release or assignment$4.00 from April 29, 2022
Release of federal tax lien$3.00

Amounts come from the Recorder's fee schedule and FAQ. Underpaid filings come back unrecorded, while overpaid filings are recorded and the difference refunded. Cards carry an added charge of $2.00 for debit, or the larger of $2.00 and 2.39% for credit.

How much does the Hamilton County Auditor collect at transfer?

The Auditor lists three charges on a taxable transfer here: a state conveyance fee of 1.00 per thousand of price, a county permissive tax of 2.00 per thousand, and .50 per parcel as the state transfer fee. Ask the Transfer Desk for the total on your price.

Certain transfers skip the price-based charges. Form DTE 100 EX names reasons such as gifts within a marriage or from parent to child, passage to an heir or devisee, and deeds that merely fix an earlier recorded one. Two exemption boxes always call for an affidavit of facts: security for a debt, and a no-money transfer that is not a gift.

Other forms may join the packet. A seller who had the homestead reduction last year or this year files DTE Form 101, and land with an agricultural use valuation calls for DTE Form 102.

Does Hamilton County still have registered (Torrens) land?

Registered land is no longer a separate track in Hamilton County. The Board of Commissioners passed Resolution 25 on August 6, 2014 to abolish it, and since November 10, 2015 any registered land document is recorded in the traditional system at the standard $34.00 and $8.00 rates.

No new certificate of title is issued under that change. A preparer should cite the existing certificate of title as the prior instrument until the parcel has changed hands. The county notes it held more registered land than any other Ohio county, and it has put millions of registered land images online.

Tell your title agent early if your parcel was ever registered. State law bars adverse possession claims against registered land, so such a parcel's history deserves a closer look.

What older records can I view from the Hamilton County Recorder online?

The Recorder's home page opens a historic search that goes well past modern deeds. It lists grantor and grantee deed indexes for 1914 to 1988, deed books from 1794 to 1903, mortgage and mortgage release books from 1794 into the early 1900s, and mechanic lien, lease and power of attorney documents from the same early period.

  • Cemetery lot documents (1794 to 1934).
  • Church and organization documents (1794 to 1919).
  • Veteran discharge records (1794 to 1965).
  • Plat maps, a 1913 Cincinnati street index and a 1824 map of the Symmes survey.

These help a seller trace how a very old parcel was first conveyed, and they help a title examiner find an old easement or lien that never got released.

What page format does the Recorder expect on a deed?

A single statute, ORC 317.114, sets the page standard statewide, and the Recorder's FAQ links to its standardization guidelines. Off-standard deeds are still taken, with $10 plus another $10 added.

  • Type at least size ten, in dark ink without highlighter.
  • Sheets from letter size up to legal length.
  • One inch of white space at the sides and the foot.
  • Three inches left clear at the head of page one, plus one and a half inches on later pages, for county endorsements.

Releases and assignments must carry a full legal description under ORC 5301.46, and a Hamilton County deed that describes the land differently from the last recorded deed may need a boundary survey approved by the County Engineer before the Auditor will transfer it.

Does Hamilton County offer a deed fraud alert?

Yes. The Recorder's Real Estate Fraud Alert is a free notification service. If a document is recorded under an identity you are watching, you receive an email.

The office's online search, called Acclaim, lets anyone browse the index and document images without paying. For owners who live out of town or hold inherited property, signing up costs nothing and gives early warning of an unexpected filing against the parcel.

More questions about Hamilton County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Will the Hamilton County Recorder write my deed for me?

No. Blank forms are not sold there and staff cannot do searches or title work. Have a lawyer or closing agent draft the deed.

Can a deed be mailed to the Hamilton County Recorder?

Yes, once the Engineer's and Auditor's stamps are on it. Add a prepaid return envelope with your own address so the recorded deed can find its way home.

When does the Hamilton County recording desk shut?

At 3:30 PM, half an hour before the office itself closes. Items handed to the Auditor's Transfer Desk after 3:20 PM wait for the next business day.

Is one payment enough for both Hamilton County offices?

No. Each office bills separately: conveyance and transfer charges go to the Auditor, and the recording fee goes to the Recorder.

Must a new owner in Hamilton County record the deed?

In practice yes. ORC 5301.25 treats an unrecorded deed as fraudulent toward a later good-faith buyer who knew nothing of it, leaving the new owner's title exposed until the Recorder indexes the deed.

The Hancock County recorder of deeds records Ohio deeds and mortgages.

Who records deeds in Hancock County

  • Hancock County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

Fees

Selling in Hancock County?
We buy Hancock County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Hancock County by the numbers

Hancock County ranks 34 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 74,885 people in 33,871 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $196,500, the median home value sits 7% above the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Hancock County reports $69,699. Owner-occupancy is 69%, so renters hold about 31% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1972, about 51 years ago.

Where in Findlay do Hancock County deeds get filed?

The filing counter is at 300 S. Main Street, Room 23, Findlay, Ohio 45840, and the number to call is 419-424-7091. Doors are open weekdays from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm. The day's recordings end at 4:00 pm, so a document delivered later waits for the following business day.

Walk-in, mail and electronic filing are all accepted. A mailed package should hold the document, payment, a return envelope with your address, conveyance forms if ownership is changing hands, and recording instructions where the filing calls for them.

What does Hancock County look like on paper?

Northwest Ohio's Hancock County spans 531 square miles of land and counts Findlay as both seat and largest city. The General Assembly organized it in 1828 out of the southern part of Wood County and named it for John Hancock. Its neighbors are Wood, Seneca, Wyandot, Hardin, Allen, Putnam and Henry counties.

The 2020 count was 74,920 residents, and the July 2025 estimate of 75,034 shows almost no movement. Roughly 70.8% of households own the home they live in.

  • Typical home value among owners: $204,700 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median household income of $73,141, and a poverty rate of 9.0%.
  • 34,342 housing units, and 361 permits pulled during 2025.
  • Average commute: 18.0 minutes, shorter than in Hamilton County.

Numbers are from QuickFacts for Hancock County, and Wikipedia supplies the founding and neighbors.

How did Hancock County's recording fee change in 2025?

A $5 increase took effect January 1, 2025, bringing the first two pages to $39 while added pages stay at $8. The Recorder's fee page credits Senate Bill 94 and cites ORC 317.32.

ItemAmount
First two pages of a deed, mortgage or lease$39
Each additional page$8
Marginal entry$4
Copies, assisted, per page$2
Copies, unassisted, per page$0.15
Non-conforming document (ORC 317.114)$20
Federal tax lien, and its release$5 and $3

Figures are from the Recorder's fee schedule page. Payment is by cash or check only, never card. Make the check out to the Hancock County Recorder and write a second check for the Auditor.

What goes to the Hancock County Auditor with a deed?

According to the Recorder's FAQ, the Auditor's conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand and the transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. A deed that changes ownership stops at the Auditor before the Recorder, and the two offices coordinate so the transfer and recording line up.

ORC 319.202 has the buyer or the buyer's representative file the value statement. It counts the full consideration paid or to be paid, mortgage and vendor's lien included, as the value, and it forbids willfully falsifying that figure. An exempt transfer needs only a statement of the reason.

If the land had a homestead reduction or an agricultural valuation, ask the Auditor which extra forms apply, since the statute has the buyer question the seller on both.

What risk comes with an unrecorded Hancock County deed?

A deed left unrecorded loses ground to a later buyer. ORC 5301.25 sends deeds to the recorder of the county where the land lies, and until that happens they are fraudulent against a subsequent good-faith purchaser with no knowledge of them.

The same statute deals with surveys. When land being conveyed was surveyed, the Auditor requires the surveyor's name in the deed, in a line reading "A survey of this property was made by" and then the name.

  • File within days of closing.
  • Staple nothing: keep the Auditor's endorsement and the returned copy in one folder.
  • Compare the new legal description line by line with the prior deed.

Why is indexing so central at the Hancock County Recorder?

By the Recorder's own description, land records must stay current, legible and easy to reach, and indexing is what lets a searcher find each one. With it an examiner can assemble a chain of title, the line of ownership, and see debts or encumbrances against the land.

The page lists the public, attorneys, historians, genealogists and title examiners as users. It also explains that some Ohio counties hold Torrens registered land, whose boundaries are certified and whose title a state insurance fund guarantees. For a seller here, a tidy deed history keeps a title search short, while a gap can delay closing.

How do I get a copy of a Hancock County deed or plat?

There are three routes to a copy of a deed or mortgage: come to the office, phone with your name and address so staff can locate it, or search the website for anything recorded since January 1, 1985. Staff-assisted copies cost $2 a page, and copies you make yourself cost $0.15 a page.

  • Plats 24 by 36 inches: $50 a page.
  • Plats 11 by 17 inches: $40 a page.
  • Township zoning resolutions: $50, and zoning amendments: $20.

Those figures come from the Recorder's January 2025 schedule.

How do Hancock County's townships show up in deed descriptions?

The county began in 1828 as Findlay Township alone, with Amanda and Welfare (now Delaware) added that April. Jackson came in 1829, Liberty and Marion in December 1830, and Big Lick, Blanchard and Van Buren in 1831. Washington, Union and Eagle were laid out in 1832, Cass and Portage in 1833, Pleasant in 1835, Orange in 1836, Madison in 1840 and Allen in 1850.

In 1845 part of the southeast corner went to the newly formed Wyandot County. Farmland outside Findlay is often described by township, so deeds for those parcels will cite these units. Check that your new deed repeats the description from the deed you received.

Can I look up Hancock County land records myself?

The Recorder's online search holds documents recorded and imaged from January 1, 1985 to the present, and historical indexes can be viewed online as well. Enter names last name first, such as Doe John, and enter companies as they normally appear.

A search cannot be run by parcel number at the Recorder's office. You need the owner's name and the legal description. If you lack either one, start at the Hancock County Auditor's website to find the owner and parcel details, then return to the Recorder.

The county is indexed alphabetically online only for 1985 to the present, and anything earlier has to be searched in the office. The Recorder will also provide copies by phone, in person or through the website.

Can I e-record a deed in Hancock County?

Yes. Electronic filing is accepted for every document type, including deeds that must pass the Auditor's conveyance step. The office works with four outside submission services.

E-recording suits title firms, lenders and law offices best. A homeowner can simply ask whoever handles the closing whether the deed will be sent electronically.

More questions about Hancock County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Will the Hancock County Recorder add or remove a name on my deed?

Not without a new deed. The Recorder says adding or removing someone, or changing a name, takes a newly prepared deed, and the office only records documents. It suggests an attorney or title office to prepare it.

Who holds my original deed after I pay off my mortgage in Hancock County?

Neither the Recorder nor your bank holds the original deed during the loan. You should get it back shortly after closing, so contact the attorney or title office that handled the sale. If it is lost, the Recorder can make a copy.

Does the Hancock County Recorder provide blank deed forms?

No. The office does not give out blank deeds, mortgages, liens or other real property forms, and it recommends an attorney or title office for preparation.

How much is the Hancock County conveyance fee?

The Recorder's FAQ lists $3.00 per thousand for the Auditor's conveyance fee and $0.50 per parcel for the transfer fee. Confirm the total with the Auditor before you pay.

What time must I get a deed to the Hancock County Recorder?

By 4:00 pm. The office stays open until 4:30 pm, but recording for the day ends at 4:00 pm and later filings are recorded on the next business day.

Where is the Hardin County Recorder in Kenton?

The Hardin County Recorder is at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220, Kenton, Ohio 43326. Dial 419-674-2252 or 419-674-2250, or fax 419-675-2802. The counter opens at half past eight and closes at four on weekdays.

The Auditor is in the same courthouse, Suite 250, at 419-674-2239, and keeps hours of 8:00 to 4:00 on weekdays. Since a conveyance has to touch both offices, a short walk down the hall is often how a deed gets done.

The Recorder's page links to an online search run through Kofile, and it points visitors to the Ohio Recorders' Association site for more fee information. The office also says plainly that it keeps the vital records of land ownership and of every lien against it, which is why a clean recorded deed matters to the next buyer.

What is Hardin County, Ohio, made of?

Hardin County lies in west central Ohio and Kenton is both seat and biggest city. The legislature created it in 1820, it was organized in 1833, and its name honors John Hardin, a Revolutionary War officer. Land area comes to 470 square miles and borders Hancock, Wyandot, Marion, Union, Logan, Auglaize and Allen counties.

It is a small, mostly rural county. The 2020 census put 56.4% of residents in rural areas, and the population has slipped from 32,058 in 2010 to 30,696 at the 2020 count and about 30,072 by July 2025.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 74.7% (2020 to 2024).
  • Typical owner-reported home value: $151,200.
  • Median gross rent: $793, and 12,944 housing units.
  • Median household income: $62,484, and mean commute of 23.6 minutes.
  • Building permits in 2025: 24.

Numbers come from QuickFacts for Hardin County, and Wikipedia supplies geography and founding.

What do Hardin County's housing numbers mean for a seller?

The 2020 census counted 12,883 housing units in the county, with 9.7% of them vacant. Of the occupied homes, 71.3% were owner-occupied and 28.7% rented, with 10.0% of rentals sitting empty. There were 11,638 households, and about 28.3% of them were people living alone.

In a county with this many single-person households and a falling population, a house that sits listed for a while is not unusual. A sale to someone paying cash and closing at a local title office still ends with the same Auditor stamp and the same Recorder filing, so the deed steps in this guide apply to either route.

Why must a Hardin County deed carry the Auditor's stamp?

A mailed conveyance is taken only when the Auditor's stamp is already on it. The office says it will not walk a conveyance through the map department and the Auditor's office for you.

That sets the order: map department and Auditor first, Recorder last. A seller who mails a deed straight to the Recorder should expect it to come back unrecorded. A seller who lives far away can hand that errand to the attorney or title agent running the closing.

On the Auditor's forms page you will find the DTE 100 value statement, the DTE 100EX exemption statement and the DTE 101 homestead conveyance statement, with a reminder to confirm the newest version with the Ohio Department of Taxation.

What does a Hardin County recording run?

The recording fee comes from state statute, and the Recorder's page refers readers to the state recorders' association for rates. ORC 317.32 builds the opening pair of pages from a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee, with $4 and $4 for each page that follows.

The statute also lets a county charge a document preservation surcharge of up to $5. The Recorders' Association table, revised October 24, 2024, lists $34.00 up front for two pages and $8.00 for each extra page, and notes a surcharge not exceeding $5.00 per document may be added. Call the Hardin County Recorder at either of its two numbers to learn exactly what the county adds per document, and keep the receipt with your closing papers.

ItemState table amount
Recording, opening two pages$34.00 (surcharge up to $5.00 may apply)
Recording, each additional page$8.00
Marginal notation$4.00
Certified copy$2.00 per page and $1.00 per seal
Document not meeting format standard$20.00
Release of federal lien$3.00

Source: the Ohio Recorders' Association table and ORC 317.32. Pay the Recorder for recording, and expect separate Auditor charges.

What must happen to a deed before Kenton will record it?

The seller signs and then acknowledges the deed in front of an authorized official. Under ORC 5301.01 that can be a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, who certifies the acknowledgment.

Many sellers visit a notary at a title company or bank. The deed then goes to the Auditor with a completed DTE 100, or a DTE 100EX for an exempt transfer. Ask the Hardin County Auditor for the conveyance rate and per-parcel transfer fee, since counties differ.

ORC 317.114 sets the page format here as in every Ohio county: legible print, black or blue ink, no highlighting, and empty space at the head of the page for county stamps.

What does the Hardin County Auditor handle for a manufactured home sale?

Homes of the manufactured or mobile kind that are taxed like real property use their own set of forms. The Auditor posts a registration certificate (DTE 41), a conveyance fee statement of value and receipt (DTE 100M), and an exemption statement (DTE 100MEX) for that category.

A refund or waiver application for destroyed or damaged manufactured homes (DTE 49) is posted too. When the home sits on land you own, ask the Auditor whether your sale takes the real property forms, the manufactured home forms, or both.

The Real Estate section adds the 2 1/2% reduction application (DTE 105C), the valuation complaint (DTE 1) and a deduction application for damaged or destroyed property (DTE 26). Ask about the 2 1/2% reduction at closing if the buyer will make the house a primary home.

How do Hardin County tax dates affect a sale?

The Auditor acts as the county's chief assessor, and its page describes a full reappraisal of real property every six years with an update every three. Find out where your parcel sits in that cycle, because a new value can change the tax bills a buyer inherits.

On the Auditor's calendar, February 11 is the last day to pay the first half of the real estate bill without penalty and July 8 is the last day for the second half. The same calendar opens the Board of Revision complaint period on January 3 and closes it March 31. Homestead and 2 1/2% rollback applications are listed as due in early June. Check your current tax bill for exact dates, since weekends and holidays can move them.

  • Learn from the closing agent how taxes will be prorated.
  • Ask whether the parcel has a homestead reduction, because DTE 101 then travels with the deed.
  • Photograph the stamped deed before it goes to the Recorder.

More questions about Hardin County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Can a deed go by mail to the Hardin County Recorder?

Only if the Auditor's stamp is already on it. Without that stamp the Recorder's Office will not take the conveyance, and it does not walk deeds through the map department or Auditor.

When is the Hardin County Recorder open?

It opens at half past eight each weekday morning and closes at 4:00 p.m., at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220 in Kenton.

Who can notarize a deed in Ohio?

Under ORC 5301.01 a notary public, a county auditor, a county engineer, a mayor, or a judge or clerk of a court of record can take the acknowledgment. Most sellers use a notary.

Is there a Hardin County online records search?

Yes. The Recorder's page links to an online service and search provided through Kofile.

Who tells me the Hardin County conveyance fee?

The Auditor, at 419-674-2239. That office collects the conveyance and transfer fees before the deed moves on to the Recorder.

Where is the Harrison County Recorder in Cadiz, and what are its hours?

The Harrison County Recorder's Office is at 100 West Market Street, Cadiz, Ohio 43907. The phone is 740-942-8869 and the fax is 740-942-4693. The office is open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., excluding holidays.

Recording stops at 4:15 p.m. Anything received between 4:15 and 4:30 goes on the next day's business. A recorded document comes back by mail in about two to three working days, and a self-addressed stamped envelope is required for every mailing.

The office does not furnish forms, and only completed documents are recorded. Staff inspect each document and try to have errors corrected before filing.

What is Harrison County, Ohio, like for owners of land?

Harrison County is a rural county in eastern Ohio, with Cadiz as the seat and largest village. It was formed in 1813 from parts of Jefferson and Tuscarawas counties and borders Carroll, Jefferson, Belmont, Guernsey and Tuscarawas counties. The Recorder's page describes a county of 15 townships and 9 villages.

It has about 402 square miles of land and is among the least populous counties in the state: 14,483 people at the 2020 census and an estimated 14,070 in July 2025, a drop of 2.9% from the 2020 base. In the 2020 census, 100.0% of residents lived in rural areas.

  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $121,500 (2020 to 2024).
  • Owner-occupied rate: 76.3%, with 7,361 housing units.
  • Median household income: $54,414, and 25.5% of residents are 65 or older.
  • Mean commute: 29.4 minutes, longer than the commute figures for Hamilton, Hancock or Hardin counties.
  • Building permits in 2025: 2.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts for Harrison County and Wikipedia for county history.

Why do Harrison County deeds need preapproval?

Since October 1, 2022, every transfer is preapproved before recording. The Harrison County Auditor and Engineer adopted minimum requirements for instruments of conveyance so that land is described accurately for tax purposes.

The steps run through three offices, and all three must finish before the deed is recorded:

  1. Submit an unsigned copy of the deed, not the original meant for recording, with a completed Document Conveyance Form. It can go by email to the Map Office, by mail, by delivery or in person.
  2. Wait at least four days while the Map Office, the Auditor and the Recorder review it and return it with any changes explained.
  3. After approval, bring the signed documents in person, by mail, by delivery or to the dropbox. The Map Office forwards them to the Auditor, and the Auditor sends them on to the Recorder.

The Auditor's goal for its own part is 24 hours, though workload can stretch it. If you hand in several documents, say in what order they should be processed.

What does the Harrison County Auditor charge on a transfer?

The Auditor's page lists a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, with no rounding, and a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel. Both are due before the transfer is approved. The Auditor accepts check or cash only.

Under ORC 319.202 the grantor pays the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, while the grantee files the value statement. Every transfer needs a named seller and buyer, an accurate legal description with the full parcel numbers, and a stamp of approval from the Map Office.

  • DTE Form 100 declares value on a taxable transfer.
  • DTE Form 100EX explains the reason on an exempt one.
  • DTE Form 101 is required if the parcel participates in the homestead reduction.
  • DTE Form 102 is required if the parcel participates in the agricultural valuation program.
  • A DTE Attachment Sheet helps when many parcel numbers will not fit on the form.

Splits and combinations of parcels need Auditor preapproval and a minimum of three days. Those requests are made by form and emailed, since they are no longer taken in person.

What does the Harrison County Recorder charge?

The Recorder's fee page prints $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each page after that, citing ORC 317.32. It also explains that half of all recording fees go to the state for the Ohio Housing Trust Fund.

ItemFee printed by the Recorder
Recording, first two pages$34.00
Recording, each additional page$8.00
Marginal reference by separate instrument$4.00
Certified photocopy$2.00 per page, plus $1.00 for the seal
Photocopy of a record, from the overview page$2.00 per page
Plat, minimum fee$40.00

Source: Harrison County Recorder fee page and office overview. State law has been amended since that page was written, and ORC 317.32 now permits a document preservation surcharge of up to $5. Call the office to confirm the total before you write a check. The overview page says veterans are entitled to free certified copies.

What do the abbreviations on Harrison County deeds mean?

The Auditor's transfer page lists common deed types with short codes that appear in county records. Knowing them helps you read a chain of title.

  • WD is a General Warranty Deed, and QC is a Quit Claim Deed.
  • ED is an Executor's Deed, AD an Administrator's Deed and FD a Fiduciary Deed.
  • TD is a Trustee's Deed, and SD is a Sheriff's Deed.
  • SV is a Survivorship Deed, and TO is a Transfer on Death Designation Affidavit.
  • CD is a Corrected Deed or re-recording, and MD is a Mineral Deed.
  • AF is an Affidavit, AT an Affidavit Relating to Title, and RW a Right of Way or Easement.

A seller who inherited the house will often hold an ED, AD or TO in the chain. A buyer's title agent will want that document and the preceding ones in order.

What else is in Harrison County besides farmland and wells?

The Conotton Creek Trail, a paved rails-to-trails path of 11.4 miles, runs along Conotton Creek from Bowerston to Jewett in the northern part of the county. The Recorder's office also serves on the county records commission, which decides how long county records are kept and when they may be disposed of.

The Recorder collects document fees for the county's general fund and each year notifies the county commissioners and township trustees of their duty to file zoning resolutions, maps and amendments. Those zoning filings can matter to a seller with land in one of the 15 townships.

Do mineral rights show up on Harrison County deeds?

They can. Harrison County sits over the Utica shale, which drew attention as a tight oil zone, and the county's history includes oil finds near Jewett in 1895 and the Scio area in 1898. Because of that, a deed may reserve or convey minerals separately from the surface.

The Auditor's list of common deed types includes a Mineral Deed, along with the General Warranty Deed, Quit Claim Deed, Survivorship Deed, Transfer on Death Designation Affidavit and others. The state recorders' fee table also lists a claim to preserve mineral interests as a recordable item.

  • Ask the title company whether minerals were reserved in an earlier deed.
  • Ask whether any oil and gas lease is of record on the parcel.
  • Make sure the new deed states exactly what is conveyed.

Where can I search Harrison County property records online?

The Recorder lists an online records search through Kofile's CountyFusion and a newer cloud search at harrison.oh.publicsearch.us. A Property Alert service is also listed on the Recorder's page.

If you ask for copies by mail, the Recorder charges $2.00 per page, and payment is due before the copies are sent. To find a record, give the owner's name, the volume and page, or the subdivision, lot, township, range and section.

More questions about Harrison County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How long does Harrison County preapproval take?

A minimum of four days. The Map Office, Auditor and Recorder all review the unsigned copy before returning it with any needed changes.

What does Harrison County charge per thousand dollars of price?

The Auditor lists $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, without rounding, plus $0.50 per parcel, payable by check or cash.

What time does the Harrison County Recorder stop recording?

4:15 p.m. Documents received after that until 4:30 p.m. are recorded the next business day.

Does the Harrison County Recorder supply deed forms?

No. The Recorder's office does not furnish forms. The Auditor adds that it does not prepare deeds and recommends a legal representative for a transfer.

Can veterans get copies of discharge papers in Harrison County?

Yes. The Recorder's overview says veterans are entitled to free certified copies, and certified copies of DD214s go to funeral homes.
