How do you avoid the extra $20 charge at the Lawrence County recorder?

Prepare the deed to the layout in section 317.114, which covers documents prepared after June 30, 2009. Per the office's guideline page, a deed that misses it costs $20.00 more. Its checklist:

  • Computer type of at least 10 point.
  • Sheets between 8.5 by 11 and 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Black or blue ink only, with no highlighter.
  • One inch of margin on both sides and the bottom of each page.
  • A 3 inch strip at the top of page one that only the recorder, auditor and engineer may use, then 1.5 inches at the top of later pages.

Court and taxing authority papers, plats, DD214 discharges, state or federal documents and older instruments fall outside the rule. A margin guidelines PDF on the site helps whoever drafts the deed.

What happens at the Lawrence County auditor before a deed reaches the recorder?

The auditor is at 111 S Fourth Street, phone (740) 533-4310, open weekdays 8 to 4. Under section 319.202, the buyer files a statement of value, the seller pays the conveyance fee and the auditor endorses the deed.

The state charge in section 319.54(G)(3) is $1 or ten cents per $100, whichever is more, and a county can add a transfer tax capped at thirty cents per $100 under section 322.02. Counties choose their own totals, so the quickest check is the Conveyance Fee Calculator in the Tools menu of the auditor's site, which includes the parcel transfer fee. Type in a parcel count and a sale price, and it returns a charge.

Which Lawrence County records can you search?

The recorder's home page sets out coverage. The current index runs from 1982 for deeds, 1988 for mortgages, 1989 for financing statements and 1981 for leases, liens and miscellaneous records. A second online index reaches much further back.

  • Deed grantor and grantee entries date from 1818 to 1984, and mortgages from 1834 to 1988.
  • Plats are listed from 1818 to 2010, and leases from 1864 to 1981.
  • Index books online include deed volumes 1 through 475 and mortgage volumes 82 through 441.
  • Odd corners of the archive include veterans grave plats and a soldiers discharge index covering 1864 to 1865.

Staff will help with a search during business hours. A title search that stops at the 1982 deed index can miss older easements, so ask where the older books begin for your parcel.

What should a seller know about Lawrence County itself?

This is the southernmost county in Ohio, part of Appalachian Ohio and the Huntington-Ashland metropolitan area, with part of Wayne National Forest inside its lines. It touches Cabell and Wayne Counties in West Virginia and Boyd and Greenup Counties in Kentucky. Formed December 20, 1816 from parts of Gallia and Scioto, it moved its seat from Burlington to Ironton in 1851, and the present courthouse dates to 1908. County histories date the first settlers to Hanging Rock on the Ohio River in 1796.

Census QuickFacts for Lawrence County: 55,710 people in mid 2025, which is 4.3 percent fewer than in April 2020. Housing units, 26,564. Owner occupancy, 72.3 percent. Typical value of an owned home in 2020 to 2024, $144,000. Median gross rent, $848. Median household income, $58,325, with 15.0 percent of residents in poverty. Builders took out 23 permits in 2025.

How did House Bill 186 change second half 2025 bills in Lawrence County?

The auditor's home page says the Inflation Cap Credit appears on second half 2025 real estate bills, which were mailed July 9, 2026. It is based on new revenue each school district gained from the 20 mill floor measured against inflation, and it did not alter any appraised value. A buyer or title agent can view the credit by searching the parcel on the auditor's site.

An owner who paid before the credit was applied needs to do nothing, because any overpayment rolls into the 2026 first half bill. Ask the auditor how a carried credit should show on a closing statement.

Which tools does the Lawrence County auditor offer sellers?

Beyond the calculator, the auditor's Tools menu holds a Tax Estimator, a Sales Report, a Sales List and a Delinquency Report. The sales reports list recent sales in the county, which helps when you set a price. The auditor's site also carries a GIS parcel viewer through its map link, and a search page that shows the appraisal and payment history for any parcel.

More questions about Lawrence County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Where do I record a deed in Lawrence County, Ohio?

At the Lawrence County Recorder, Court House, 111 South 4th Street, Suite 21, Ironton, OH 45638, phone 740-533-4314. Stop at the county auditor first so the statement of value and conveyance fee are handled.

How much does the Lawrence County recorder charge for a deed?

The fee notice shows $39.00 for one or two pages and $8.00 for each page after that, effective January 1, 2025. $4.00 reference fees and the $20.00 standardization charge apply when triggered.

Is there a way to estimate the Lawrence County conveyance fee?

The auditor's website has a Conveyance Fee Calculator, with parcel count and sale price as inputs, and the page says it includes the parcel transfer fee. The auditor's office at (740) 533-4310 can confirm a figure.

What happens if my deed breaks the Ohio margin rules?

The recorder accepts it and adds $20.00. The 3 inch top margin on page one is reserved for the recorder, auditor and engineer. Court papers, plats, DD214s, state or federal documents and older instruments are exempt from the rule.

How far back do Lawrence County deed records run online?

The current index lists deeds from 1982 forward, and the older online index lists grantor and grantee entries from 1818 to 1984. Index books include deed volumes 1 through 475. Ask the recorder about anything the online index does not reach.

Licking County by the numbers

Licking County ranks 17 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 180,311 people in 73,021 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $250,700, the median home value sits 37% above the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Licking County reports $81,033. The median home was built in 1978, about 45 years ago.

Where does a Licking County deed get recorded?

Deeds and mortgages for Licking County land go to the recorder's office at 20 S. Second Street in Newark, OH 43055. The recorder's page shows (740) 670-5300 for calls and (740) 670-5303 for fax, with the counter open from 8 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays and recording running from 8:30 AM to 4:15 PM.

The office examines each document, assigns it a unique document number and a recording time, and uses that time to fix the order in which filings were made. Its records reach back to the early 1800s. Anyone can search the paper index and record books at the counter for no charge, and staff will help with the search.

Online viewing covers a window of more than two decades. A recorder's news item says documents recorded since September 22, 1997 can be viewed over the internet, including deeds, mortgages, releases, assignments and UCC statements. The same item looks back at 1999, when the office recorded 50,826 documents, among them 8,598 deeds and 13,895 mortgages, which it called its busiest year to that point.

What does recording cost in Licking County?

The county posts its own recording sheet, and its formula reads: number of pages times $8, plus $23. A marginal reference costs $4. The fees page also announces a $5 preservation surcharge per document for standard document types as of January 1, 2025. Ask the recorder how the surcharge appears in your total before you write the check.

Licking County recording fees as printed on the county sheet
Document lengthFee
1 to 2 pages$39.00
3 pages$47.00
4 pages$55.00
10 pages$103.00
20 pages$183.00
30 pages$263.00
Marginal reference$4.00

Source: Licking County recording fees sheet. Other charges come from the Ohio Recorders' Association fee table the county also posts: photocopies and plat copies are $1.00 plus $1.00 per page, a certified copy is $1.00 plus $1.00 per page with a seal fee of 50 cents plus 50 cents, and a document that fails the state layout rules adds $10.00 plus $10.00.

Which documents does a Licking County recorder see around a house sale?

The state fee table groups a long list of instrument types under the basic page charge. These are the ones most tied to a sale, a payoff or an inheritance:

  • Warranty deeds, quit claim deeds, survivorship deeds and limited warranty deeds.
  • Executor's, administrator's, guardian's, trustee's and sheriff's deeds.
  • Certificates of transfer and transfer on death designation affidavits.
  • Mortgages, assignments, modifications, satisfactions and releases of lien.
  • Affidavits on facts relating to title, affidavits of surviving spouse and affidavits of successor trustee.
  • Memoranda of trust, powers of attorney, land contracts and easements.
  • Mechanic's liens, lis pendens notices and Medicaid estate recovery liens and their releases.

Military discharges and veteran grave summaries record without a fee under the same table. Federal tax liens carry their own listed charge of $5.00.

What happens at the Licking County auditor before the recorder?

No deed skips the auditor. Under section 319.202 the grantee, or an agent, declares the value conveyed, and the auditor stamps the deed with the fee. An exempt transfer needs only a stated reason.

Per the auditor's page, since May 1, 2026 a conveyance, exempt transfer, split or merge has to arrive by 4 p.m. to clear that day. That office is at 20 South Second Street, (740) 670-5040.

Sellers pay the state conveyance fee there. A county real property transfer tax would be collected at the same counter only if commissioners had enacted one under section 322.02, at no more than 30 cents per $100. Learn from the auditor whether it exists before choosing a closing date. When it does exist, payment precedes the trip to the recorder.

How can you search and watch Licking County records?

The recorder publishes a PaxWorld public access site at apps.lickingcounty.gov. It asks users to create an account with a username and password. Images that a user buys download to the user's computer, so the site tells visitors to allow downloads in the browser.

The same page promotes an AlertMe service that sends a notification when a document is recorded in your name. Older records can be searched at the recorder's counter, where the index is free.

Title companies, law firms and banks that file often can use eRecording. The county's page names four vendors:

  • CSC eRecording Solutions
  • ePN, the eRecording Partners Network
  • Indecomm Global Services
  • Simplifile

The recorder says electronic filing can cut turnaround from three to five working days to minutes or hours, and payment of recording fees is handled electronically.

What does the Census Bureau report about Licking County housing?

The Census Bureau QuickFacts table tallies 73,930 housing units for July 2025 and 68,620 households across the 2020 to 2024 survey years. Owned homes are valued around $275,200, and about three in four are lived in by the owner. Rent averages $1,078, and a homeowner with a loan pays about $1,693 monthly.

Population rose from 178,501 in April 2020 to an estimated 185,564 in July 2025. Newark is the county seat, and Wikipedia lists Heath, Johnstown, New Albany, Pataskala and Reynoldsburg as the other cities.

How does a payoff or an inheritance show up in the Licking County record?

A sale usually produces more than one recorded paper. The buyer's deed goes on record, and the seller's old mortgage is cleared by a satisfaction or release that the lender files. The state sheet lists satisfaction, release, partial release and cancellation as separate document types, and a marginal reference costs $4 when the recorder notes a link to an earlier filing.

Inherited property follows a different path. An executor's or administrator's deed, a certificate of transfer or a transfer on death designation affidavit can move title without a conventional sale, and each one is recorded like any other deed. If the owner received Medicaid benefits, the state table also lists a Medicaid estate recovery lien and its release as recordable instruments. Anyone who spots one of these in the chain should raise it with the title company before closing.

Veterans can record a military discharge with the recorder. The recorder's page names veterans discharges among the documents it accepts, and the state fee table shows no charge for a military discharge. Census data counts 11,370 veterans in Licking County for 2020 to 2024.

What should you know about Licking County's boundaries when searching old deeds?

The legislature carved Licking County out of Fairfield County in 1808, so the earliest history of a parcel may sit under the parent county's name. The recorder's holdings go back to the early 1800s, and the staff will help a searcher read the index. Seven counties touch Licking County, which means a parcel near a county line can carry a description that mentions Knox, Delaware, Franklin or another neighbor.

A rural parcel adds another wrinkle. The county ranks 11th among Ohio's 88 counties for farm products sold, and Wikipedia reports frequent developer offers for farmland near New Albany. A deed search for acreage should cover every transfer and any easements. The state table lists agricultural easements and conservation easements as their own document types.

More questions about Licking County, OH Recorder of Deeds

When is the Licking County recorder open?

Staff are in from 8 AM until 4:30 PM on weekdays, and recording itself happens between 8:30 AM and 4:15 PM. Call (740) 670-5300 before a holiday.

What would a two-page Licking County deed cost to record?

The county sheet lists $39.00 for one to two pages, and its formula is pages times $8 plus $23. A third page brings the printed fee to $47.00.

Is searching Licking County records free?

Searching the index and record books at the recorder's counter is free. The online PaxWorld site requires an account, and purchased images download from the site.

Do I need the auditor before I record a Licking County deed?

Yes, the auditor endorses the deed and collects the conveyance fee first. For same-day processing the deed must reach the auditor by 4 p.m.

Can a title company e-record in Licking County?

Yes, the recorder accepts electronic filings through four listed eRecording vendors. Recorded documents come back electronically.

Who records deeds in Logan County

  • Logan County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Document filing fees: first 2 pages $39; each additional page $8; non-standardization fee $20; marginal references $4 each.
  • Recorder document search via CountyFusion (kofiletech.us) linked from county site; e-recording not seen.

Fees

Selling in Logan County?

Logan County by the numbers

Logan County ranks 52 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 46,140 people in 23,797 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $186,200, the median home value sits 2% above the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Logan County reports $69,183. Owner-occupancy is 78%, so renters hold about 22% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1973, about 50 years ago.

Which Bellefontaine office accepts a Logan County deed?

The Logan County recorder sits in the annex at 100 S. Madriver Street, Bellefontaine, OH 43311. The recorder's page gives 937-599-7201 as the phone number and lists the office as open Monday through Friday from 8:00 until 4:30. Wednesday is the day the office issues Veteran ID cards.

The office describes itself as keeper of the land ownership record and of every lien against land. It lists work under more than 1,000 Revised Code sections, stores records in archival form and indexes each filing so a searcher can trace ownership forward in time. Title examiners, attorneys, genealogists and historians all use those files.

The Logan Online portal lists a Recorder's Document Search for looking up filed documents. The recorder also publishes Document Standardization Guidelines, a historical page and a Veteran ID Card Program page.

What does the Logan County recorder charge?

A short schedule appears on the county's recordable documents page. Everything the recorder collects goes into the county general fund.

Logan County document filing fees
ItemFee
First 2 pages$39
Each additional page$8
Non-standardization fee$20
Marginal reference, each$4

Source: Logan County Recordable Documents.

Phone 937-599-7201 for a total on a lengthy document.

What layout rules can trigger the $20 fee in Logan County?

The extra $20 applies to paper that ignores Ohio Revised Code 317.114. Logan County's guidelines page ties the rule to documents prepared after June 30, 2009, and spells out the specifications:

  • Type no smaller than 10 point.
  • Sheets between letter size and legal size, meaning 8.5 by 11 up to 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Ink in black or blue, with no highlighter marks.
  • One inch of white space along both sides and the foot of each page.
  • Three inches blank at the head of page one, held for stamps from the recorder, auditor and engineer.
  • An inch and a half blank at the head of every later page.

Five categories fall outside the rule: papers from a court or a taxing authority, plats, DD-214 discharge forms, state or federal documents, and anything signed before the law took effect. The page also offers a downloadable template.

What does the Logan County auditor do before the recorder?

A deed visits the county auditor first, and that office shares the 100 S. Madriver Street address. The auditor's forms page names the paperwork that can come into play:

  • Conveyance Form DTE 100 for an ordinary sale, and DTE 100M for a manufactured home.
  • Exempt Conveyance DTE 100EX, or 100MEX for a manufactured home.
  • Agriculture Conveyance DTE 102.
  • Homestead Conveyance DTE 101.
  • Owner Occupied Credit Application DTE 105C and the Homestead Exemption Application DTE 105A.
  • Destroyed Property Application DTE 26 for a building that no longer stands.

Logan County also posts a Survey and Conveyance Standards PDF for legal descriptions and an online Conveyance Fee Calculator. The state conveyance fee falls on the grantor under section 319.202, and a county transfer tax joins it only where commissioners adopted one under Chapter 322. The auditor can say which charges apply to your sale.

How does a Logan County forfeited land sale reach the recorder?

A parcel that went through tax foreclosure and drew no buyer in two offerings is forfeited to the State of Ohio and remanded to the auditor. The auditor's published auction rules describe a sale at the Logan County Courthouse Annex, 100 S. Madriver Street. Properties sell "As-Is" and "Buyer Beware," and the auditor gives no representation about possession, eviction or prior inspection.

The high bidder gets an Auditor's Deed. According to the rules, the auditor files it with the recorder and delivers it to the purchaser, and ownership passes at the moment the deed is delivered to the recorder. That deed extinguishes earlier title except for taxes and assessments not yet due, federal tax liens, easements and covenants running with the land. The rules bar a delinquent taxpayer or a current owner of the parcel from buying.

Bidders pay everything or leave at least $1,000 per parcel on sale day, and the remainder is due within 10 calendar days. The 2021 version of the rules also adds a 50 cent per parcel transfer charge and a 50 cent per parcel charge for envelope and postage, on top of recording.

When do Logan County property taxes come due, and how often is value reset?

The treasurer's site gave July 22, 2026 as the second-half due date and counted 38,426 parcels. The office sits at 100 S. Madriver Street, Suite D, and answers at (937) 599-7223 on weekdays between 8:00 AM and 4:30 PM. A county FAQ also describes an automatic withdrawal option that pulls the bill from a bank account on the last due date.

The auditor's FAQ lays out the cycle: a reappraisal each six years and a possible adjustment in the third calendar year after it. Taxable value is 35 percent of appraised value. The Ohio Department of Taxation's schedule puts Logan County in a 2028 update and a 2031 reappraisal. Formal complaints go to the Board of Revision, which accepts them from January 1 through March 31. Three officeholders sit on the board, the auditor, the treasurer and the president of the commissioners, or their representatives, and an owner can bring appraisals or comparable sales to the hearing.

What do county history and Census data say about Logan County?

Logan County lies in west central Ohio. The recorder's history page says it was cut from northern Champaign County in 1818 and named for Benjamin Logan. Hardin County was carved out of its northern portion in 1820 and began running its own affairs in 1833. Bellefontaine is the seat and only city, and Wikipedia places Campbell Hill, Ohio's highest natural point at 1,549 feet, northeast of the city.

Survey figures for 2020 to 2024 appear in the Census Bureau QuickFacts table:

  • Population reached 46,302 in July 2025, a 0.3 percent change from April 2020.
  • Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $203,200, and 77.6 percent of housing is owner-occupied.
  • Monthly owner costs: $1,326 with a loan, $601 without.
  • Rent at the median: $845 gross.
  • The 19,560 households report a median income of $71,551.
  • 24,071 housing units stood in the county in July 2025, and 120 permits were issued in 2025.

What is the recorder's role in Ohio, and what is Torrens land?

The recorder's history reaches back to the Northwest Territory of 1787, which gave every county such an office. Statehood in 1803 brought a rule that common pleas judges name the recorder. Voters took over the choice in 1829, and a four-year term has applied since 1936.

The recorder's page also covers Torrens registration. Where land is registered under the Torrens Act, its boundaries are certified and a state insurance fund backs the title, and the recorder handles those registered land records. A seller who owns an unusual rural tract should ask the Logan recorder whether any part of it was registered.

The auditor, the treasurer and the recorder all list 100 S. Madriver Street in Bellefontaine as their address, so a closing agent can take the transfer, the tax question and the recording to one building.

More questions about Logan County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the filing fee for a short Logan County deed?

The posted schedule charges $39 for the opening two pages, then $8 for every page after that. A document that misses the layout standards picks up $20 more.

When can I visit the Logan County recorder?

The office at 100 S. Madriver Street in Bellefontaine opens weekdays at 8:00 and closes at 4:30. Its phone number is 937-599-7201.

Which papers skip the Logan County layout fee?

Court and taxing authority papers, plats, DD-214 discharge forms and state or federal documents are exempt, along with anything executed before the law began.

Does the Logan County recorder help fill out deed forms?

The office keeps and indexes records. Have a title company or attorney draft the deed, and phone 937-599-7201 with filing questions.

When does a forfeited land buyer own the property in Logan County?

Ownership passes when the auditor hands the Auditor's Deed to the recorder, according to the published auction rules. The auditor then sends the recorded deed to the purchaser.

Lorain County by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts 314,588 people and 135,584 housing units in Lorain County, which ranks 9 of 63 oh counties here. Median home value is $207,200, which is 13% above the middle county in this oh set. Households here earn a median $70,693; the middle oh county is at $69,699. 26% of occupied homes are rented, which leaves 74% owner-occupied. The median home was built in 1972, about 51 years ago.

Which Elyria office files a Lorain County deed?

The Lorain County Recorder files it. The office is in Room 102 at 226 Middle Avenue, Elyria, OH 44035, answers 440-329-5148, and posts weekday hours of 8 AM to 4 PM on its website.

The Recorder keeps the land record and nothing else. Its FAQ page says staff do not supply blank forms, fill them in, alter a deed, decide ownership disputes, or search for liens for you. A title company or attorney covers those jobs. The same page says county records go back to 1824, and that you can download a free copy of your own deed from the online property search, with certified copies available at the counter.

What is the Lorain County Recorder's fee for a deed?

Two pages of a deed cost $39.00 on the Recorder's 2026 fee page, and the price climbs by $8.00 with every added page. Each printed side is a page, so a deed printed on both faces of two sheets counts as four.

Lorain County Recorder, 2026 charges for common filings
FilingCharge printed
Deed, mortgage, lease or affidavit, pages one and two$39.00
Page three and beyond, per page$8.00
Release, amendment or assignment (marginal notation)Recording fee plus $4.00 per notation
Plain copy$2.00 per page
Certified copy$2.00 per page, plus $1.00 for the seal
Real estate financing statement$12.00, plus $4.00 for each name indexed
Federal tax lien and its release$5.00 and $3.00
Living will or health care power of attorney$34.00 minimum, $40.00 maximum

The page explains that the amount splits evenly between a basic fee and a contribution to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, and reports $1,402,515 contributed in 2025. A notice dated 01/01/2026 credits a $5.00 preservation surcharge from Senate Bill 94 for the present level. Its sample chart shows three pages at $47.00, five at $63.00 and ten at $103.00.

What happens at the Lorain County Auditor before recording?

The Auditor endorses the deed first. Section 319.202 of the Revised Code has the buyer file a value statement, then the Auditor marks the fee on the deed. The seller pays it.

The Auditor's transfer page lays down rules that trip up late arrivals:

  • Transfers happen Monday through Thursday, 8 AM to 4 PM, so Friday closings need planning.
  • E-filed packets are cut off at 3 PM, and walk-ins at 4 PM.
  • Since November 1, 2012 the office has refused anything sent through the U.S. Postal Service.
  • Handwritten forms go back to the sender. Typed, fully completed forms only.
  • A packet with a missing form or the wrong payment is returned, never held.

Staff may not fill out the conveyance or exempt form or give advice about it, citing section 4705.01. Your closing agent or attorney should assemble the packet and confirm the amounts with the Auditor's office in advance.

How is the conveyance fee set in Lorain County?

Ohio law fixes the base at a one dollar minimum, or ten cents for each $100 or fraction of $100 of value, whichever is more, in section 319.54(G)(3). A county commission may add a transfer tax of as much as thirty cents per $100 under section 322.02. Phone the Auditor for the combined Lorain County rate before you estimate your net proceeds.

Many transfers owe no conveyance fee, though the form must say why. Common cases for families include gifts between spouses or from parents to children, deeds among heirs of one estate where no money is paid, and moves into or out of a revocable trust. Every transfer, exempt or not, also pays fifty cents for each parcel.

What formatting rule can add $20 to a Lorain County filing?

Documents prepared after June 30, 2009 must meet the standardization rules of section 317.114, and the Recorder adds $20.00 when they miss. Its fee page spells out font size, ink color, paper size, a three inch blank band on page one and margins on every side, and offers a downloadable template. Court papers, plats, DD-214 discharges and state or federal documents are exempt.

Have the preparer check the template before signing, since a rejected deed costs a second trip to Elyria. The Recorder does not help complete forms, so the preparer is your only safeguard here.

What does Lorain County look like for a seller?

Lorain County stretches along Lake Erie west of Cuyahoga County. Of its 923 square miles, 432 are water, or 47 percent, according to Wikipedia. Elyria holds the courthouse, while the city of Lorain has the most residents. Amherst, Avon, Avon Lake, North Ridgeville, Oberlin, Sheffield Lake and Vermilion complete the list of cities.

On its QuickFacts page, the Census Bureau estimates 323,219 residents in July 2025 and 139,777 housing units. Its 2020 to 2024 survey shows a typical owned home worth $223,200 and a typical household income of $73,347. Owners live in 74.0 percent of homes. Median gross rent was $966, and the mean commute was 25.4 minutes. Most Lorain County sales therefore involve an owner-occupied house with a deed and mortgage already on file.

How can a Lorain County owner guard against deed fraud?

Sign up for the free property alert service offered on the Recorder's website. The FAQ describes deed fraud as criminals transferring a property without the owner's knowledge and advises owners to check their records and be wary of unsolicited deed offers.

Before you list a house, search your own parcel online and confirm the last recorded deed carries the name of the person who will sign. If an old mortgage was paid off but its release never reached the record, have it recorded, at the $4.00 marginal notation charge.

Does the Lorain County Recorder keep veterans' discharge papers?

Yes. According to the FAQ, a veteran can record a DD-214 or NGB-22 so a safe copy exists if the original is lost. The records are protected, and only the veteran or an authorized person can see them. The fee page lists one certified copy of a veterans service discharge at no charge.

How has Lorain County grown, and why does page count matter?

Wikipedia shows 5,696 residents in 1830, 217,500 in 1960 and 312,964 in 2020. The county was set up in 1822, became judicially independent in 1824, and is home to Oberlin College.

Since each extra page adds $8.00, ask your preparer to keep the deed brief. A reference to an older recorded document also triggers the $4.00 notation charge.

What goes in the Lorain County closing packet?

Assemble these items so neither office sends you back:

  • The signed, notarized deed, typed, with the legal description and every parcel number.
  • The right conveyance form, or the exempt form with its reason written out.
  • Payment to the Auditor for the conveyance fee and the per-parcel charge.
  • A check to the Recorder sized to the page count.
  • A check that each page is in black or blue ink and has the margins the template calls for.

Because the Auditor cuts off e-files at 3 PM on transfer days, line up the vendor early on the day you close.

More questions about Lorain County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What does Lorain County charge to record a deed?

The 2026 fee page prints $39.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 per page after that. A $4.00 notation applies to each release or assignment, and a layout violation adds $20.00. The Auditor's conveyance fee is paid separately.

Will the Lorain County Auditor take a deed by mail?

No. Mailed transfers have been refused since November 1, 2012. Deliver the packet in person Monday through Thursday or send it through an approved e-file vendor before 3 PM.

Can the Lorain County Recorder fix a mistake on my deed?

No. The Recorder says it cannot alter a deed and is not trained to search for liens for you. An attorney can prepare a corrective deed, which the Recorder then files.

Who bills property tax in Lorain County?

The County Treasurer and County Auditor, according to the Recorder's FAQ. The Recorder only keeps the documents that show who owns the land.

Where can I see an old Lorain County deed?

Use the online property search on the Recorder's website to view and download a free copy. Records reach back to 1824, and certified copies are available in person.

Lucas County by the numbers

Lucas County has about 428,748 residents and 200,764 housing units in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, number 6 by population among the 63 oh counties we cover. The median owner-occupied home is worth $155,200, 15% below the median of the oh counties covered. Median household income is $60,095, against $69,699 for the middle oh county. Owners live in 62% of occupied homes and renters in 38%. The median home was built in 1962, about 61 years ago.

Where is the Lucas County Recorder, and how do I submit a deed?

The Lucas County Recorder works from One Government Center, Suite 700, in downtown Toledo, OH 43604. The Recorder's page gives 419-213-4400 for the counter and Recorder@co.lucas.oh.us for email, with weekday hours of 8 AM to 4:30 PM. Electronic recording stops at 4 PM.

Three submission routes are listed: walk it in, mail it, or e-record through a partner company. The office says it strongly encourages electronic recording or mailing, and it names CSC, ePN and Simplifile as the e-recording partners. If you mail a deed, include a self addressed stamped envelope or add return postage to the payment. The fee page accepts cash or a check payable to the Lucas County Recorder.

What does recording a deed cost in Lucas County?

The Lucas County recording fee schedule sets the basic fee at $39.00 for the first two pages of a deed or mortgage, and $8.00 for every extra page. The Recorder's news item says the $5.00 increase behind that figure took effect April 1, 2026 under Senate Bill 94, and the schedule lists $39.00 as a minimum.

Selected lines from the Lucas County Recorder fee schedule
ItemAmount shown
Deed or mortgage, first two pages$39.00 minimum
Each additional page$8.00
Non-compliant document (ORC 317.114)$20.00 per document
Reference for a marginal notation (release, assignment)$4.00 per reference

There is no reference fee on a master mortgage reference. Plats are priced by size, at ten cents per square inch with a $40.00 minimum per page, and the schedule lists three common sheet sizes with their totals.

What does the Lucas County Auditor charge before the deed is recorded?

Lucas County's Auditor publishes a real estate transfers fact sheet with two charges. The transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. The conveyance fee is $4.00 for every $1,000 of the sale price, and some transfers outlined in law are exempt from it.

The sheet adds that transfers caused by a death, adding survivorship, or placing the property into your own trust are generally exempt and cost only the $0.50 per parcel. The Auditor cannot prepare a deed, and the sheet recommends hiring an attorney because a wrong detail can get the document rejected or cause trouble years later. The Auditor's main line is 419-213-4406.

The statewide rules behind these steps are in section 319.202, which requires the buyer's value statement before the Auditor endorses a deed, and section 319.54, which lists the exempt transfers.

How can I check a Lucas County deed online?

The Recorder's page says recorded documents after 1985 can be viewed through its Online Recordings tool, which is run by a document technology vendor. The Auditor's fact sheet points to the AREIS property system, where deeds and transfers are public.

AREIS shows how title is held, which helps when you are sorting out a sale after a death:

  • Property held in survivorship carries the code ORSURVTC after the owners' names.
  • Property held by a trustee shows the word Trustee after the name.
  • A transfer on death confirmation appears as document type OD on the Transfers page.

For records from before 1985, call the counter on 419-213-4400 and ask how to request a copy.

Why should I avoid paid deed retrieval companies in Lucas County?

Because the county sells the same copy for far less. The Recorder's news section warns residents about solicitations from document retrieval companies that quote $49.50 to $87.00 for a certified copy of a deed. It adds that copies of all land records are available from the office, often for as little as $2.00.

The fee schedule backs that up: assisted copies are $2.00 per page and a certification is $1.00 per document. A copy order form can be emailed to the Recorder or faxed to 419-213-4284 if you have an escrow account with the office. Copies are paid by cash, check or escrow account only.

What does Lucas County look like for a house seller?

Lucas County covers 596 square miles of northwest Ohio, of which 255 square miles is water, along Lake Erie and the Maumee River, based on Wikipedia's county entry. Toledo is the county seat and largest city. The other cities are Maumee, Oregon, Sylvania and Waterville, and the villages include Holland, Ottawa Hills, Whitehouse and Swanton. Much of the land lay within the Great Black Swamp before settlement. I-75, I-475, I-280 and the Ohio Turnpike cross the county.

The Census Bureau reports 423,347 residents in July 2025, down 1.8 percent from the 2020 base, and 201,974 housing units. For 2020 to 2024 it shows a median owner-occupied value of $163,900, median household income of $62,224, owner occupancy of 62.0 percent and median gross rent of $934. With nearly four homes in ten rented, many Lucas County sales involve a tenant-occupied house.

Which documents does the Lucas County Recorder file besides deeds?

The office's overview lists the full range of paperwork it accepts for the permanent land record:

  • Certificates of transfer, deeds and land contracts.
  • Mortgages, liens and real estate financing statements.
  • Plats and powers of attorney.
  • Military service discharges, and any other document made recordable by the Revised Code.

For lien paperwork the schedule gives $5.00 for a federal tax lien, $3.00 for its release and $4.00 for a personal tax release. Bureau of Workers' Compensation liens and releases carry no fee. The e-recording partners also list direct lines: CSC at 866-652-0111, ePN at 888-325-3365 extension 11234, and Simplifile at 800-460-5657 extension 1031.

How did Lucas County's recording fee reach its present level?

The Recorder's news section tracks two jumps. On October 17, 2019, the state budget raised the fee for most documents by $6.00, to $34.00 for the first two pages, with half of all recording fees going to the Ohio Housing Trust Fund. The later $5.00 increase came from Senate Bill 94 and brought the figure to $39.00, under section 317.32.

The office also posted a postage change for mailed recordings. From August 17, 2026, the postage for a standard one ounce first class letter rose from $.80 to $1.00, and that amount should be included whenever no self addressed stamped envelope is enclosed. Counting a mailed deed's return postage in the payment avoids a delay at intake.

How did Lucas County come to exist, and why does it matter for a title search?

Lucas County was organized in 1835 and named for the governor of Ohio at the time. Its creation was tied to the Toledo War, because both Ohio and Michigan Territory claimed a strip of land along the border. Earlier, the Battle of Fallen Timbers took place near present day Maumee in 1794.

For a seller, the practical point is that a title company orders the ownership search. The Recorder's online system covers documents recorded after 1985, so ask the title company how it will pull anything older.

More questions about Lucas County, OH Recorder of Deeds

How much is the basic recording fee in Lucas County?

The schedule lists $39.00 for the first two pages of a deed or mortgage, with $8.00 for each additional page. A document that breaks the state layout rules draws a $20.00 non-compliance fee, and each reference for a marginal notation costs $4.00.

What are the Lucas County transfer and conveyance fees?

The Auditor's fact sheet shows $0.50 per parcel as the transfer fee and $4.00 for every $1,000 of the sale price as the conveyance fee. Transfers due to death, survivorship or moving the property into your own trust are generally exempt from the conveyance fee.

Does the Lucas County Recorder accept mailed deeds?

Yes. The Recorder encourages mailing and e-recording. Include a self addressed stamped envelope or add return postage to the payment, and make the check payable to the Lucas County Recorder.

Is there a fee to record a veteran's discharge in Lucas County?

No. The fee schedule lists no fee to record a DD-214 or to get certified copies of it from the Recorder.

Can the Lucas County Auditor prepare my deed?

No. The Auditor's fact sheet says the office cannot prepare transfer documents, including deeds, and recommends hiring an attorney. Staff can answer questions about the transfer process at 419-213-4406.

Madison County by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts 44,126 people and 16,361 housing units in Madison County, which ranks 54 of 63 oh counties here. Median home value is $231,400, which is 26% above the middle county in this oh set. Households here earn a median $83,229; the middle oh county is at $69,699. 24% of occupied homes are rented, which leaves 76% owner-occupied.

Where does a Madison County deed get recorded?

In London, at the courthouse. The Madison County Recorder sits at 1 N Main St, Room 40, London, OH 43140, and takes calls at 740-852-1854. The counter opens at 8 AM and closes at 4 PM on weekdays, though recording ends at 3:30 PM, so a deed handed over at 3:45 waits until the next business day.

Electronic recording is available through four named platforms: CSC eRecording (866-652-0111), Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox. Ask your title company or attorney which platform they use, since the deed can then be recorded without a trip to the courthouse.

What is the recording fee in Madison County?

A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00, a schedule in effect since January 1, 2025 per the Recorder. Senate Bill 94 added a $5.00 surcharge to most documents, the page explains, to fund the preservation and digitizing of records and the office's running costs, and it points to section 317.32.

That statute shows how the amount is built: half base fee, half housing trust fund fee, plus an optional county surcharge. Copies, certified copies, references to older documents and zoning filings carry their own listed amounts. Phone 740-852-1854 to price any unusual document before you mail payment.

How far back do Madison County's online land records reach?

Different record types start at different dates, according to the Recorder's own note. Checking the right category saves a trip to the courthouse:

Online coverage listed on the Madison County Recorder's page
Record typeCoverage stated
DeedsScanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 to present
Mortgages, indexingIndexed from July 17, 1964
Mortgages, imagesScanned and indexed from September 25, 1968
Miscellaneous, lease, lien, federal tax lien, mechanics lien, unemployment compensation lien, mortgage releaseHistorical Archive online, dating to at least 1980, some older

All the original books remain in the office. If a search turns up a gap, call the counter and ask staff to follow up in the books.

What does the Madison County Auditor do with a deed first?

Ohio makes the Auditor endorse the deed before the Recorder files it. Under section 319.202, the buyer's representative submits a statement of value, or a statement of the exemption reason, and the Auditor notes the conveyance fee on the deed itself.

The Madison County Auditor is at 1 N Main St, PO Box 47, London, OH 43140-0047, phone 740-852-9717, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM. Its property transfer forms page lists the packet pieces a closer may need:

  • DTE 100, the conveyance fee statement of value and receipt.
  • DTE 100EX, the statement of the reason for an exemption.
  • DTE 101, a statement of conveyance of homestead property.
  • DTE 102, a statement of conveyance of current agricultural use valuation property.
  • DTE 100M and DTE 41 for manufactured or mobile homes.
  • Affidavits of trustee and successor trustee under sections 317.22 and 5302.171.

The Auditor's site also carries a conveyance fee calculator under its Tools menu. Run your sale through it, or phone the office, rather than guessing at the county's rate.

How does the Auditor treat sale price and gifts?

For an arm's length sale, the Auditor's measure under section 319.202 is everything paid or promised, including any mortgage balance the buyer takes over. For a gift, the measure shifts to what the house would sell for on the open market. Misstating either figure on purpose is unlawful.

The buyer's statement also answers two questions. Was the seller asked whether tax reductions for owner occupancy or homestead apply? Was the land under the agricultural use valuation? A yes to either needs a sworn instrument attached. If the house is a rental, the endorsement points the buyer to a landlord filing under section 5323.02.

Which free tools does the Madison County Auditor's website offer sellers?

The Auditor's home page invites visitors to search any parcel by owner, address or parcel number to see its appraisal and payment history. A menu of tools sits beside the search box, and several help a seller price and plan:

  • A sales report and a sales list of recent transfers.
  • A delinquency report.
  • A conveyance fee calculator and a tax estimator.
  • A levy estimator, plus a GIS parcel viewer reached from the map link.

Office hours are 8 AM to 4 PM on weekdays, and the number to call is 740-852-9717.

Which rules govern conveyance fee amounts in Madison County?

Two statutes work together. Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the state charge at a dollar or a dime per hundred, whichever is bigger. Section 322.02 lets commissioners layer on a local tax up to thirty cents per hundred, owed by the grantor.

Exemptions cover several family and estate situations:

  • Gifts within a marriage, or handed down to a son or daughter.
  • Transfers among the heirs of one decedent when nobody pays money.
  • Moves into or out of a revocable trust.
  • A corrective deed that fixes an earlier recorded deed.

The exemption reason belongs on the form.

What is Madison County like around London?

Madison County lies in central Ohio west of Franklin County, with London as the seat and largest city. Wikipedia gives the area as 467 square miles with almost no water, and places the county in the Columbus metro area. Interstates 70 and 71 cross it on the way to Columbus, and a sliver of Dublin lies inside the county line.

QuickFacts puts Madison County at 46,985 residents in mid-2025, up 7.1 percent since the 2020 base, with 17,383 housing units. Over 2020 to 2024, a typical owned home was valued at $250,100 and a typical household earned $87,045. Owners occupy 77.5 percent of homes, rent runs a median $943, and the mean commute runs 24.9 minutes. The Auditor has also finished a countywide reappraisal for tax year 2026, with tentative values shown for each parcel on its website, so sellers should look up their own parcel before setting a price.

Who else works in Madison County, and what borders it?

London is the seat and the largest city. Madison County was established in 1810 and named for James Madison. In 1850 it counted 10,015 residents, mostly in farming, and in 2020 it counted 43,824. Wikipedia also lists the Ohio Peace Officer Training Academy and the state Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation among its institutions.

Neighbors include Union and Champaign counties to the north and northwest, Franklin County to the east, Pickaway to the southeast, Fayette to the south, and Greene and Clark to the west. An owner with land across a county line needs a separate recorder and auditor filing in each county.

More questions about Madison County, OH Recorder of Deeds

When does Madison County stop recording each day?

3:30 PM. The office is open until 4 PM on weekdays but stops recording at 3:30, so deliver deeds earlier in the afternoon or use an e-recording service.

What is Madison County's price for recording a deed?

A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00, a schedule in effect since January 1, 2025 per the Recorder. Check with the office for extra charges that apply to references, copies or special filings.

Can I e-record a deed in Madison County?

Yes. The Recorder names CSC eRecording, Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox as the electronic routes. Ask your title company or attorney which one they use.

Does the Madison County Auditor have a form for a trust or estate transfer?

Its forms page lists DTE 100EX for exemption reasons and affidavits for a trustee or successor trustee under Revised Code sections 317.22 and 5302.171. An attorney should pick the right ones for your situation.

How old are Madison County's scanned deeds?

Deeds are scanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 forward, according to the Recorder. Mortgages are scanned and indexed from September 25, 1968, and the original books stay in the office.

Who records deeds in Miami County

  • Miami County Recorder records deeds and mortgages.

Fees

Selling in Miami County?
We buy Miami County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Miami County by the numbers

Miami County has about 109,549 residents and 47,028 housing units in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, number 25 by population among the 63 oh counties we cover. The median owner-occupied home is worth $209,200, 14% above the median of the oh counties covered. Median household income is $74,175, against $69,699 for the middle oh county. Owners live in 73% of occupied homes and renters in 27%. The median home was built in 1970, about 53 years ago.

Where does a Miami County deed get recorded?

Deeds for Miami County property are recorded at the Recorder's Office, 201 West Main Street, Troy, OH 45373. The office answers at (937) 440-6040, takes faxes at (937) 440-6034, and is open weekdays from 8 am until 4 pm, per its county page.

The Recorder keeps the permanent chain of title: deeds, mortgages, easements, leases, plats and veteran discharges. Valuation and tax collection sit elsewhere. The county's Recorder Resources page says the Auditor sets values and assessments and the Treasurer collects taxes, while the Clerk of Courts handles property disputes. Annual volume runs to 15,169 documents, including 6,259 deeds and 4,319 mortgages, and 9,806 of the total come in electronically.

What does the Miami County Recorder charge to record a deed?

Page one and two together cost $39.00, then $8.00 for every page added, according to the office's documents and fees page. Included in that price is a $5.00 preservation fee, and the office passes a share of each fee to the state's housing trust fund, citing sections 317.32 and 317.36.

Miami County sample recording fees, effective January 1, 2025, from the Recorder's fee page
Document lengthRecording fee
1 or 2 pages$39.00
3 pages$47.00
4 pages$55.00
6 pages$71.00
10 pages$103.00

Other charges that can land on a sale or a payoff:

  • A $4.00 marginal notation fee on mortgage releases, assignments and modifications.
  • A $20.00 fee when a document breaks the Ohio standardization guidelines.
  • No fee to record or copy a military discharge (DD-214).

Enclose a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself if you mail the original.

What approvals come before the Recorder in Miami County?

A deed must clear the County Engineer and the Auditor first. Miami County's conveyance standards, adopted August 12, 2025, say every instrument is approved for transfer by the Engineer's Office, with a signed DTE 100 value statement or a DTE 100EX exemption form turned in alongside it.

Three rules in those standards matter to sellers:

  • No transfer is approved when the grantor never appears as an earlier grantee, unless the deed or an affidavit under section 5301.252 explains the gap in the chain of title.
  • A deed that carves a piece off an existing parcel, or changes the legal description, needs a boundary survey plat that the Engineer reviews.
  • Anyone claiming an exemption must prove it to the Auditor. If doubt remains, the fee is charged or the parcel does not transfer.

The Auditor's fee comes from section 319.54: $1, or ten cents per $100 of value if that is larger. Separately, section 322.02 lets county commissioners levy a transfer tax that tops out at 30 cents on each $100. Sellers pay both. Call the Miami County Auditor to learn which applies before you build a closing statement.

What else does the Miami County Recorder file, and at what price?

Deeds are one entry on a long list. The recorder's fee page names affidavits, easements, land contracts, leases, mechanic's liens, notices of commencement, powers of attorney, sheriff's deeds, survivorship deeds, trust documents and warranty deeds among the items it accepts. A few carry their own prices:

  • Federal tax lien: $5.00 to file and $3.00 to release.
  • Release of a personal property tax lien: $4.00.
  • Financing statement: $12, plus $4 for each name indexed.
  • Living will or durable power of attorney for health care: $28 minimum, $40 maximum.
  • Plats: ten cents a square inch, minimum $40.00.
  • Faxed pages: $2 local or toll-free, $4 long distance.

Sellers most often meet the mortgage release. If a lender never recorded one after an old payoff, the lien still shows on the record, so ask the title agent to check before the buyer's lender does.

What does the Miami County value statement ask the seller?

The buyer's statement under section 319.202 records whether the seller expects a reduced tax bill, such as the homestead or owner-occupancy credit, and whether the land was enrolled in the agricultural use valuation. A yes on either needs a sworn paper that both sides have accounted for the amount.

Farm ground is worth a question in a county that covers 410 square miles and has only five cities. If a seller's acreage was enrolled, leaving the program can trigger a recoupment charge, and the buyer and seller are expected to account for it before the Auditor endorses the deed.

For a rental, the Auditor's stamp also reminds the buyer to file landlord information with the Auditor under section 5323.02.

How can you look up or copy Miami County land records?

The county's records search page offers a free basic search by last and first name, or business name, in the AVA database. Images carry a watermark, and a watermarked copy is not accepted for recording.

  • Basic search: free to view and print, with a watermark.
  • Clean copies: email or call the Recorder's Office; since January 2026 copies cost $2.00 per page, paid in advance.
  • Credit cards: a service fee of $2.00 or 2.65% applies, whichever is greater. Cash and check are also taken.
  • Title searchers: Laredo Anywhere, run by Fidlar Technology, reaches deeds back to the county's start in 1807.

Deeds from 1807 through 1979 are scanned as whole books. Records for 1980 through 2008 are only partly indexed, and for anything before 1980 the county asks you to contact the office. A certified copy is $2.00 a page, and each seal adds $1.00.

Can a title company e-record a Miami County deed?

E-recording exists, but the county describes it as a tool for businesses that file regularly, not for one-time submissions. Its e-recording page lists five vendors: ePN, Simplifile, Hopdox, Indecomm and CSC. Each sets its own pricing, so a title agent signs up with a vendor directly.

A private seller closing without a title company can send the deed by mail or hand it over at the window. Ask the Recorder's Office at (937) 440-6040 whether your document type can go electronically before you plan around it.

What should a Troy-area owner know about Miami County itself?

Founded March 1, 1807 and named for the Miami people, the county seats its government in Troy. Per Wikipedia, it covers 410 square miles in the Dayton metro area and borders Shelby, Champaign, Clark, Montgomery and Darke counties. Its cities are Troy, Piqua and Tipp City, plus slices of Huber Heights and Union.

QuickFacts puts the 2025 headcount at 112,634, a 3.5% gain on the 2020 base, spread over 47,930 housing units. Roughly three in four homes are lived in by their owners (73.4%). Median home value stands at $229,100 and median household income at $76,817 in the 2020 to 2024 survey period. Commuters average 22.0 minutes to work, and the county issued 340 building permits in 2025.

A sale of any kind, from a tidy listing to a tenant-occupied fixer, follows one path here: Engineer, Auditor, Recorder.

More questions about Miami County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the address of the Miami County Recorder?

The office sits at 201 West Main Street in Troy, OH 45373. Call (937) 440-6040; it is open weekdays from 8 am until 4 pm.

What is the Miami County deed recording fee?

Two pages cost $39.00, which includes a $5.00 preservation fee, and every extra page adds $8.00. A $4.00 marginal notation fee applies to mortgage releases, assignments and modifications, and a $20.00 fee applies when a document misses the Ohio standardization rules.

Who covers the conveyance fee when a Miami County house sells?

The seller settles it with the Auditor before recording. State law sets the minimum at $1, rising to ten cents per $100 on larger values, and a local transfer tax may be added if the commissioners adopted one. The Auditor can tell you what applies to your parcel.

Does Miami County need a survey to split a parcel?

Yes. The county's conveyance standards require a boundary survey plat when a deed cuts up an existing parcel or changes its legal description, and the County Engineer reviews it before the Auditor accepts the deed.

Can I print my deed for free in Miami County?

Yes. Anyone can pull up and print a watermarked image through the basic records search without paying. A copy without the watermark must be requested from the Recorder's Office and costs $2.00 per page.

Selling in Montgomery County?

Get My Cash Offer →

Montgomery County by the numbers

Montgomery County ranks 5 of 63 oh counties in this guide by population, at about 535,528 people in 252,475 housing units (Census Bureau, 2019-2023). At $167,400, the median home value sits 9% below the oh county median for this guide. The oh county median income is $69,699, and Montgomery County reports $64,403. Owner-occupancy is 62%, so renters hold about 38% of occupied homes. The median home was built in 1966, about 57 years ago.

Where is the Montgomery County Recorder's Office in Dayton?

The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building, 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Per the county's Recorder FAQ, the full deed and index collection, 1805 to the present, is kept there on books and microfilm.

Older material sits at the County Records Center and Archives, 117 South Main Street, 6th floor, reached by the Main Street elevator, at 937-225-6366. The office records, scans and indexes paperwork on the day it arrives, whether it comes by mail, over the counter or from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department. Documents go back in the mail the next business day, and the office works from 8 am to 4 pm on weekdays.

The Recorder is one of Ohio's oldest county offices. Ohio's General Assembly made it a required county office in 1803, the year Montgomery County was founded. Judges appointed the first recorders, and voters began electing them in 1829. Today the term is four years.

What does recording a deed cost in Montgomery County?

The county's own pages show two figures, so confirm the current one with the office before you bring a check. The Recorder FAQ quotes $34.00 for the first two pages and $8.00 for each added page. The eRecording page quotes $39.00 and $8.00.

Montgomery County recording charges as printed on two county Recorder pages
ChargeRecorder FAQeRecording page
First two pages$34.00$39.00
Each added page$8.00$8.00
Mortgage release or assignment, marginal notationNot listed$4.00
No clear 3-inch top margin on page one$20.00 standardization feeStandardization laws apply

The gap matches the statute. Section 317.32 sets $17 plus a $17 housing trust fund fee for two pages, which is $34, and lets a county add a preservation surcharge of up to $5. Pay at the counter in cash, or by check or money order made out to Montgomery County Recorder.

What must a Montgomery County deed contain?

The county lists the elements a clerk checks at the window. A deed needs:

  • The names of the buyers and sellers.
  • A legal description, which you can get from the Copy Center.
  • The sellers' signatures.
  • A preparation statement, if the deed was notarized in Ohio.
  • A Transfer or No Transfer stamp from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department, plus the Engineer's approval where the property calls for it.

Notarization follows the law of the state where the signer stood. The notary block has to show a statement, a signature and an expiration date. A mortgage adds the loan amount and the lender and borrower names.

Changing a name on a deed means a new deed, a stop at the Auditor for a stamp and then the Recorder. No new deed is generated when a loan is paid off. The lender records a Release or Satisfaction of Mortgage instead.

Which Montgomery County transfers must visit the Auditor first?

Anything that conveys land passes through the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department before recording. Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement, and the grantor pays the fee set in section 319.54, plus any transfer tax the county commissioners have levied.

The county's eRecording rules draw the line clearly. Mortgages, assignments and releases with no transfer can go in electronically through Simplifile. Deeds and anything needing a No Transfer stamp, such as a transfer on death designation, an easement or an affidavit that references a deed, must be mailed or walked through the Auditor's department first.

The Auditor and Engineer also publish conveyance standards, adopted August 2, 2021, governing legal descriptions and splits. Copies are on the Auditor's third and fifth floors and the Engineer's eighth floor at 451 West Third Street.

How do you find or print a Montgomery County deed?

Print any document you find on the Recorder's online search at no charge. If you cannot print, the Copy Center charges $2.00 per page, and certification adds $1.00. The office does not run title searches, but the 5th floor Public Research Area has public computers for doing your own.

  • Deeds, releases and liens are searchable by name on the county's online system.
  • To trace an older house, build the chain of owners from the grantee-grantor or tract index, then check the Auditor's tax lists for a jump in value that suggests new construction.
  • Veterans who recorded a DD214 can request a copy at no charge, and the Recorder issues a free Veteran ID card to those who record one.

Searching by street address happens on the Auditor's site instead of the Recorder's.

How do Montgomery County records help trace an older house?

The county's FAQ lays out a research route for anyone curious when a house was built. Start with the chain of ownership in the Recorder's deed records, using either the alphabetical grantee-grantor index or the tract index, which is organized by legal description. Both index types run from 1805 to the present, with deed books and microfilm for 1935 on and microfilm for 1805 through 1934.

  • At the Records Center and Archives, the alphabetical indexes cover 1805 to the present, and tract index microfilm covers 1805 to 1934.
  • The Auditor's tax lists run 1803 to 1954 as indexes and 1955 to 1985 as original books.
  • A jump of more than 50% in one year's taxable value usually points to construction or improvements.

The FAQ adds that taxable values were recorded at 35% of market value since 1973, and at 40 to 45% before that. The county says the research is the individual's job, though the archives answer questions at 937-225-6366. The Recorder's computerized tract index, one of few in-house systems of its kind, earned a National Association of Counties achievement award, and new records are indexed the day they arrive.

What is Montgomery County like for a house seller?

Dayton is the county seat, and the county spans 464 square miles in southwest Ohio, according to Wikipedia. It touches Miami, Clark, Greene, Warren, Butler, Preble and Darke counties. Besides Dayton, the cities include Kettering, Huber Heights, Centerville, Miamisburg, Vandalia, Trotwood and Englewood, and the villages are Farmersville, New Lebanon, Phillipsburg and Verona.

The county reports roughly 230,000 parcels. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts lists 539,598 residents in 2025 and 254,375 housing units. Owners occupy 62.5% of homes, the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $180,900, and median gross rent is $1,026. Median household income is $66,139.

Because more than a third of homes are rented, many sellers here are landlords. The Auditor's deed endorsement for residential rental property reminds the buyer to file landlord information under section 5323.02, so a rental sale carries one more form than an owner-occupied home.

More questions about Montgomery County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What is the address of the Montgomery County Recorder?

The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building at 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Records Center and Archives material is at 117 South Main Street, 6th floor.

How much does Montgomery County charge to record a deed?

The Recorder FAQ prints $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 per added page, while the eRecording page prints $39.00 and $8.00. Call the office to confirm which figure applies the day you file.

Do I need the Auditor before the Recorder in Montgomery County?

Yes, for any deed. The Auditor's Deed Transfer Department stamps it Transfer or No Transfer and collects the conveyance fee, then the deed goes to the Recorder. Only non-transfer papers such as mortgages and releases can be e-recorded directly.

Is there a fee for a poorly formatted document in Montgomery County?

Yes. The Recorder FAQ adds a $20 standardization fee when page one lacks a clear 3-inch top margin, and the eRecording page says all Ohio standardization laws apply.

Can I get a free copy of my Montgomery County deed?

Yes, if you print it yourself from the Recorder's online search. The Copy Center charges $2.00 per page if you cannot print, with certification costing $1.00 more.

Fees

What we could not confirm

  • Recorder fee schedule/e-recording

Which Morgan County office takes a deed for recording?

The Morgan County Recorder's Office is in the Riecker Building at 155 East Main Street, Room 160, McConnelsville, OH 43756. The county recorder page gives 740-962-4051 for calls and recorder@morgancountyohio.gov for email.

The Auditor works from the same building and answers at 740-962-4475. A Morgan County deed does not go straight to the Recorder, though. The Auditor's FAQ sends questions about prior deeds and recording fees to the Recorder's counter on the first floor, so call that number before you drive in.

In what order do Morgan County offices handle a deed?

A deed starts at the County Engineer, moves to the Auditor, and ends at the Recorder. The Auditor's real estate FAQ applies the same route to transfer on death designations, land contracts, easements and covenants, and says Auditor staff will take your papers to the other offices in the proper order.

The Engineer's number is 740-962-3171. The county's conveyance standards want these items in or attached to any document that transfers land:

  • The parcel number.
  • A full legal description.
  • The property address.
  • A reference to the prior instrument.
  • The tax-mailing address.

Signatures must be legible, and a printed name below an unclear signature is accepted. After the Auditor finishes, the county's property website refreshes within one to two business days.

What does the Morgan County Auditor collect on a sale?

The Auditor's transfer page lists the charges that precede recording. The office takes cash, or a check made out to the Morgan County Auditor.

Morgan County Auditor transfer charges as printed on the county's transfer page
ChargeAmount
Conveyance fee$3.00 per $1,000 (sale price x .003)
Transfer fee$0.50 per parcel
Split fee, for every split$100.00

Morgan quotes one conveyance figure of $3.00 per $1,000. State law behind the Auditor's fee (section 319.54) starts at $1 or ten cents on each $100, and section 322.02 allows commissioners to levy a local transfer tax with a ceiling of 30 cents per $100. Ask the Auditor how Morgan's single number is divided if your closing statement needs a line for each. For acreage splits, call the Engineer, since the survey and the split fee start there.

What fees apply when the Morgan County Recorder records a deed?

Morgan County's published pages send recording-fee questions to the Recorder, so ask for the current sheet when you call 740-962-4051. The ceiling comes from section 317.32. Two pages carry $17 for the recorder and $17 for the housing trust fund, and each page beyond them adds $4 and $4. On top, the county may tack on a preservation surcharge, capped at $5 an instrument.

The same section prices a certified copy at $1 plus $1 per page, a counter photocopy likewise, and a marginal reference made by separate instrument at $2 plus $2. Page counts use legal-size sheets and include the caption page, which is why a third page raises the bill.

Is a Morgan County transfer taxable if no money changes hands?

It can be. According to the Auditor's FAQ, a sale is taxable, and so is a gift with no money involved unless an exemption fits. Only the relationships listed on the DTE 100EX form are exempt, and the filer reads each lettered choice to see whether one fits.

The statute lists many of those exemptions in section 319.54(G)(3), including transfers among heirs of one decedent when no money is paid and transfers to the grantor of a trust the grantor can revoke. If someone on the deed has died, the Auditor points families to Morgan County Probate Court at 740-962-2861 when there is a will, and to a title agent or real estate lawyer when a survivorship deed or transfer on death designation was recorded.

Section 319.202 (full text) also has the buyer certify what the seller said about reduced taxes and farm-use valuation. An owner who sells a home that carried the homestead reduction also files form DTE 101, the Statement of Conveyance of Homestead Property, which the Auditor's homestead page lists. Morgan's Auditor lists a $25 one-time filing fee for the farm program (CAUV), which requires crops, animals or timber on at least 10 acres.

What should a Morgan County seller expect on parcels and tax bills?

Parcel changes take effect at once, but the bills lag. After combining parcels, the owner keeps getting separate paper bills until the next tax year, and the owner of an original parcel receives the tax bill for the whole original parcel until the next year after a split. The Auditor advises raising that with a title company or real estate attorney before the sale closes.

Taxes are due in February and July, and the Treasurer at 740-962-3561 bills and collects them. Value complaints go to the Auditor between New Year's Day and the end of March. The standard Homestead Exemption exempts $25,000 of a home's market value for qualifying seniors and for owners who are permanently and totally disabled, with a $50,000 enhanced version for qualifying disabled veterans.

Why did the Morgan County Auditor change a property's value?

Value changes come from a short list of causes, per the Auditor's FAQ:

  • A full reappraisal, which Ohio law requires of every parcel once every six years.
  • A countywide update in the third year of that cycle, based on market trends.
  • New construction, as shown by local permits.
  • Corrections to square footage, bedroom or bathroom counts.
  • A Board of Revision decision, or damage to or destruction of the property.

The Board of Revision has three members: the Auditor, the Treasurer and the president of the county commissioners, or their designees. It adjusts values, not tax dollars. Ohio law generally allows one filing in a three-year period, and withdrawing a complaint still counts as that filing. Corporations should have an attorney file for them.

What does Morgan County look like on paper?

Morgan County was formed December 29, 1817, from parts of Guernsey, Muskingum and Washington counties and organized in 1819, per Wikipedia. It covers 422 square miles, and McConnelsville, Chesterhill, Malta and Stockport are its villages. The county is the third-least populous in Ohio, with 13,802 people in 2020. Neighbors are Muskingum, Noble, Washington, Athens and Perry counties.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts reports a 2025 estimate of 13,626 residents, down 1.3% from the 2020 base, and 7,437 housing units. Nearly four homes in five (78.9%) are owner-occupied, and the survey's median home value is $150,900, and median household income is $59,351. Mean travel time to work is 37.5 minutes, the longest among the three counties in that table, and 2025 saw only 23 building permits. With about 33 people per square mile, the Engineer's survey and split steps are worth planning for if you are selling part of a larger tract.

More questions about Morgan County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Where is the Morgan County Recorder located?

It is in the Riecker Building, 155 East Main Street, Room 160, McConnelsville, OH 43756. The phone is 740-962-4051.

Who do I see first when I sell land in Morgan County?

Start with the County Engineer at 740-962-3171, then the Auditor, then the Recorder. The Auditor's staff will deliver your documents to the other offices in order.

What is the conveyance fee in Morgan County?

The Auditor prints $3.00 per $1,000 of sale price, plus a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee and a $100.00 split fee for every split. Payment is by cash or a check to the Morgan County Auditor.

Is a gift of a house taxable in Morgan County?

It can be. Only the relationships listed on the DTE 100EX exemption form qualify as exempt, so read each choice on that form or ask the Auditor at 740-962-4475.

How much will Morgan County charge to record my deed?

Call the Recorder at 740-962-4051 and ask for the current sheet. The state schedule behind it is $34 for two pages, $8 for each more, and a county may add up to $5 per instrument for preservation.
