Which office in Morrow County puts a deed on record?

Morrow County deeds and mortgages are recorded at the county recorder's office inside the courthouse at 48 E. High St., Mt. Gilead, OH 43338. The recorder's page lists 419-947-3060 and a weekday counter open from 8 until 4.

Mount Gilead holds the courthouse and is the biggest village in the county, so most sellers who live in Cardington, Marengo, Edison or the townships make the same trip. Anyone who prefers not to drive can file through an electronic recording company instead (see below).

What kinds of documents does the Morrow County recorder accept?

The office's documents-filed list is broad. For a home sale or an inherited house, these are the entries you are most likely to need:

  • Deeds, including warranty, quit claim, survivorship and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgages, along with releases, assignments, assumptions and subordinations.
  • Land contracts, leases, easements and powers of attorney.
  • Trusts, affidavits and certificates of transfer.
  • Liens of several kinds, such as mechanic's liens, notices of commencement and federal or personal tax liens.

Plats, condominium filings, annexations and zoning resolutions also appear on the list, which tells you the same office holds the map side of the county's land records.

Can a Morrow County deed be filed electronically?

Yes. The recorder's page says e-recording has been open for every document type since September 8, 2025, and it names four vendors to call for help: CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm. Title companies and closing attorneys usually already hold an account with one of them, so a seller rarely needs to sign up personally.

Record searching moved to a different system in the same period. The records search page sends visitors to RecordHub, where you must create a login before you can look anything up. The county says the account costs nothing and that the login requirement was added to protect the records from cyberattacks.

What happens at the auditor's office before the recorder sees the deed?

Under section 319.20, the county auditor moves the parcel into the new owner's name and endorses the deed. Before that, the incoming owner or an agent for that owner files a statement of value as described in section 319.202, electronically or in three paper copies.

The statement carries two questions that matter to a Morrow seller. Has the property received a tax reduction for owner-occupied homes? And was the land ever enrolled in the Current Agricultural Use Valuation program? If the answer to the second is yes, the statement must note that the land can face a recoupment charge when it stops qualifying.

The Morrow County Auditor's own conveyance fee page prints $4.00 per thousand for both real estate and manufactured homes. The grantor pays it, together with the 50 cent transfer fee that section 319.54(G)(2) sets for each parcel entered.

What does Ohio charge to record a document?

The recorder has no room to set its own prices for the basic filing. Section 317.32 prescribes a base fee and an equal housing trust fund fee, and the office may tack on an optional preservation surcharge capped at five dollars, which the county keeps for general use. Payment is due when the paper is handed in, though electronic filers may settle afterward by electronic funds transfer or a similar method.

Recording charges printed in Ohio Revised Code 317.32
ItemBase feeHousing trust fund fee
First two pages of an instrument$17$17
Each added page (legal-size sheet or fraction, caption page included)$4$4
Certified copy, per page$1$1
Recorder's seal on a certification50 cents50 cents
Marginal reference, each$2$2

A long deed with several exhibits therefore costs more than a two-page one. Ask the title agent for a page count before closing so the check is the right size.

Which Morrow County transfers owe no conveyance fee?

The state statute names many transfers that skip the auditor's fee. The ones that come up most often in family and estate sales are these:

  • A deed that only corrects or confirms one already recorded.
  • A gift from one spouse to the other, or from a mother or father to a son or daughter.
  • A transfer among the heirs or devisees of one decedent where no money changes hands.
  • A deed into a trust whose maker kept an unlimited power to revoke it, and the deed back out.
  • Any transfer with no money or other valuable consideration that is not a gift.
  • A transfer made only to secure or release a debt.

When an exemption applies, the filing states the reason for it. Anyone unsure whether a family deed qualifies should phone the auditor before the paperwork goes to the recorder.

Who has to sign a Morrow County deed, and how is it witnessed?

Ohio's section 5301.01 requires the grantor to sign the deed and to acknowledge the signature before a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. In practice most sellers use a notary at the title company or a bank.

If a mortgage is being paid off from the sale, the lender's release has its own clock. Under section 5301.36, the mortgagee must record the release within ninety days of satisfaction. Check the recorder's index a few weeks after closing to confirm it appears.

How can a Morrow County owner watch for fraudulent filings?

The recorder's office offers a free fraud alert service called Property Check. A subscriber is told when a document is filed against a named property, which helps catch a forged deed or a bogus lien early. It suits anyone whose house sits empty or came through an estate, since nobody is opening the mail there.

Alerts do not replace a periodic look at the record. A quick RecordHub search under your own name every so often costs only the time it takes to log in.

How does the Morrow County housing stock look on paper?

Morrow County sits in central Ohio across roughly 406 square miles and was organized in 1848 from parts of four neighboring counties. It borders Crawford, Richland, Knox, Delaware and Marion counties and belongs to the Columbus metro area. The villages are Cardington, Chesterville, Edison, Fulton, Marengo, Mount Gilead and Sparta, and a slice of the city of Galion reaches in from the north. Ohio's center of population fell near Marengo in 2010, and the Mid-Ohio Sports Car Course draws visitors near Steam Corners.

The Census QuickFacts page for Morrow County reports a 2025 estimate of 36,305 residents living among 14,981 housing units. Owners occupy 81.2 percent of homes, with a $222,300 median value reported for the five survey years ending 2024, and workers average a 32.8 minute trip to their jobs. The county is mostly owner-held, and a long commute suggests many residents work in other counties.

What should be in the packet before a Morrow County closing?

A clean filing starts with a deed that names the grantor exactly as the prior recorded deed does. The auditor's transfer step uses a reference to the earlier recorded instrument, so a mismatch in spelling or a missing prior-deed citation can hold things up. Bring the full legal description, the grantee's mailing address and the signed statement of value.

Also confirm whether the parcel was ever in the farm-use program. The Morrow County Auditor's page says an application for that program carries a one-time $25 fee, has a filing cutoff on the first Monday of March, and that land removed from the program owes a recoupment charge equal to the savings of three years. A seller who sold off a few acres of a farm should ask the auditor how a split affects that charge.

Finally, ask the closing agent who will hand in the paperwork and by which route. A paper deed goes through the courthouse offices in a set order, while an e-recorded deed goes through the vendor's system. Knowing the route tells you when to expect the recorded copy.

More questions about Morrow County, OH Recorder of Deeds

Which number reaches the Morrow County recorder?

Dial 419-947-3060. The counter is inside the courthouse at 48 E. High St. in Mt. Gilead, and its posted weekday hours end at four in the afternoon.

Does Morrow County accept deeds filed online?

Yes, through electronic recording vendors. The recorder's page names CSC, Simplifile, ePN and Indecomm and says e-recording has covered all documents since September 8, 2025.

What is the Morrow County conveyance fee?

The county auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand. The grantor pays it at the auditor's office, along with a 50 cent per parcel transfer fee set by state law.

Do I need an account to search Morrow County land records online?

Yes. The records search now runs through RecordHub, and the county asks users to create a free login. The county explains that the step protects the records from cyberattacks.

Is a deed between family members free of the conveyance fee?

Some are. State law exempts gifts between spouses and between a parent and child, and transfers among heirs of one decedent for no money. The filing must state the exemption, so check with the auditor first.

Muskingum County by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts 86,382 people and 38,343 housing units in Muskingum County, which ranks 31 of 63 oh counties here. Median home value is $170,100, which is 7% below the middle county in this oh set. Households here earn a median $59,203; the middle oh county is at $69,699. 31% of occupied homes are rented, which leaves 69% owner-occupied. The median home was built in 1972, about 51 years ago.

Where is the Muskingum County Recorder's Office?

The Muskingum County Recorder works from 401 Main Street, Zanesville, OH 43701, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 2333, Zanesville, OH 43702. The county recorder page gives (740) 455-7107 and a weekday window from half past eight until half past four, closed on legal holidays.

The same page says the office's holdings reach back to 1803, the year before the county itself was organized in 1804. Surveyors, genealogists, attorneys and title examiners all use them.

How far back do the online Muskingum County indexes go?

Not every record type was indexed from the same year, so a search that returns nothing may only mean you are looking before the index begins. The recorder's page prints a start year for each category, and a Historical Indexes tab covers earlier material.

Online index start years printed on the Muskingum County Recorder's page
Record typeIndex begins
Deeds1977
Mortgages1976
Liens and miscellaneous1975
Leases1981
Military discharges1965
Plats1800
UCC filings1993

For anything older than those years, use the Historical Indexes tab, and look at the training sheet in the office's Forms section for instructions.

What documents does the Muskingum County Recorder file?

The documents-filed list on the recorder's page covers almost everything tied to land. The entries a seller or heir meets most often are below.

  • Warranty, quit claim, survivorship and sheriff's deeds.
  • Mortgages and every companion paper: releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and waivers of priority.
  • Land contracts, leases, easements and powers of attorney.
  • Trusts, affidavits and certificates of transfer.
  • Mechanic's liens, notices of commencement and federal or personal tax liens.

Plats, condominiums, street name changes, zoning resolutions and name changes sit on the same list.

What does the county do before a Muskingum County deed reaches the recorder?

The auditor's transfer page lays out the path. A document can be handed in at the counter, mailed, or sent through eRecording software. If the legal description uses metes and bounds, or covers something other than a full lot in a subdivision, it first goes to the County Engineer's Office on the third floor of the courthouse for approval. After that it goes to the Auditor's Office for the transfer, and only then to the recorder.

A full subdivision lot can skip the engineer and go straight to the auditor. The auditor's FAQ adds that every deed and related document must be notarized by a notary registered with the Ohio Secretary of State.

What are the Muskingum County conveyance and transfer fees?

The Muskingum County Auditor prints a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, plus a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel. State law sets a floor and a ceiling for this charge. Section 319.54(G)(3) requires $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars, whichever is greater, and section 322.02 lets commissioners add an optional tax of up to thirty cents per hundred.

The grantor, meaning the seller, pays these amounts to the auditor when the deed is delivered, according to section 319.202. The statement of value that goes with the deed is where the seller reports any owner-occupancy tax reduction or agricultural valuation tied to the parcel.

What does Ohio charge the recorder to record a deed?

The recorder's basic filing charge comes from section 317.32: a base fee of $17 for the first two pages and a housing trust fund fee of the same amount, followed by $4 plus $4 for each page after that. A document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars may be added.

Certified copies run $1 plus $1 a page, and a seal on a certification adds 50 cents plus 50 cents. The statute allows e-filers to pay after presentation by electronic funds transfer or a comparable method. The recorder can tell you which surcharge figure Muskingum County applies, so ask before you write the check.

Which transfers in Muskingum County are exempt from the conveyance fee?

Section 319.54(G)(3) excludes a long list. Sellers and heirs usually care about the following ones.

  • Gifts between spouses or between a parent and child.
  • Deeds that confirm or correct an earlier recorded deed.
  • Transfers by court order that are not the result of a sale ordered by the court.
  • Moves among heirs of the same decedent when nothing is paid.
  • Transfers into and out of a revocable trust.
  • Interests valued at $100 or less.

The statement of value must state the reason for any exemption claimed.

How can a Muskingum County owner guard against a forged deed?

Two free alert tools exist. The recorder offers Property Check, a fraud alert system that warns you about filings made on your behalf. The auditor's FAQ explains that you can also call (740) 455-7109, option 1, to have your phone number attached to your parcels so you hear when one appears on a deed to be transferred.

Anyone who suspects the ownership record has been changed should phone the auditor at that same number. The auditor says it will investigate the property record and coordinate with the proper authorities if needed.

What is the county around Zanesville like for a home seller?

Muskingum County is in east-central Ohio and is nearly split in two by the Muskingum River. Zanesville is the county seat and largest city. At 673 square miles it ranks fourth in Ohio by land area, and its 2020 population was 86,410. Neighbors include Coshocton, Guernsey, Noble, Morgan, Perry and Licking counties. Higher education is local: Muskingum University, Zane State College and an Ohio University branch campus in Zanesville.

On the Census QuickFacts table, Muskingum County lists 38,597 housing units for 2025 and a 68.2 percent owner-occupied rate. The median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $182,200, and median household income is $60,780. About one occupied home in three is rented, so many sellers here are landlords with tenants in place.

What happens to a Muskingum County deed after it is recorded?

Once the recorder indexes the deed, it appears in the online records, which the office says are refreshed each weekday. Documents are posted to the website within a reasonable time after filing, so a deed recorded this morning may not show up in a search until later in the week.

Two follow-up steps are worth doing. First, look up the parcel in the auditor's property search to confirm that the owner name and tax mailing address changed. The treasurer's FAQ says a billing address change needs a written, signed form, so a buyer who wants bills at a new address should send one. Second, when a mortgage was paid off at closing, search the mortgage index for the lender's release, since the lender has ninety days to record it under section 5301.36.

The recorder's page also carries a fair housing notice. Any deed provision that restricts the sale, rental or use of a dwelling because of race or color is invalid under federal law and cannot be enforced, which matters when you read very old deeds from the county's long record.

More questions about Muskingum County, OH Recorder of Deeds

What are the Muskingum County Recorder's hours?

Weekdays from half past eight to half past four, except legal holidays. The phone line is (740) 455-7107.

Where do I send a deed in Muskingum County?

Bring or mail it to the Auditor's Office first for the transfer, then it goes to the recorder at 401 Main Street, Zanesville. Metes and bounds descriptions need County Engineer approval before the auditor accepts them.

What is the conveyance fee in Muskingum County?

The auditor's page prints $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, plus $0.50 per parcel. The seller pays it at the auditor's office.

Can I search Muskingum County deeds online?

Yes, but the deed index starts in 1977. Older records are in the Historical Indexes tab on the recorder's site, which has its own training sheet.

Does the county offer a fraud alert for my property?

Yes. The recorder runs a free service called Property Check, and the auditor will add your phone number to your parcels if you call (740) 455-7109 and choose option 1.
